findings.field: passage.gloss (para 2), compression.note (para 2), sources[5], advocate.best_defense, module docstring
findings.problem: The p. 366 figure is attributed to a specific publication that does not contain it. The gloss states "the book reproduces the anomaly-direction map from Copi, Huterer, Schwarz & Starkman's review Large-Angle Anomalies in the CMB (Advances in Astronomy 2010:847541)"; the sources list calls that review "the review the source's p. 366 figure is taken from"; compression.note calls the Cold Spot label "a coordinate label printed inside a figure reproduced from Copi, Huterer, Schwarz & Starkman's review". I rendered the page image: the figure is a talk-slide titled "ANOMALIES SUMMARY" with the Cold Spot credited on-figure to "Cruz &al MNRAS(356)29", and the book prints no credit line for it. Copi et al. 2010 (arXiv:1004.5602, ar5iv full text) has seven figures — comoving length, C(theta) expectation, multipole vectors, quadrupole+octopole map, two two-point correlation plots, and a multiplicative-model realization — none of which is this map, and the strings "Cruz", "SG pole", "max asym" and "ANOMALIES SUMMARY" return zero occurrences in it. The entry is also internally inconsistent: sources[2] calls the same thing "the same Schwarz figure caption". On a site whose product is provenance, and which carries attribution guards in its own test suite, this is the worst available error.
findings.fix: Withdraw the attribution and use the README's third origin state — untraced rather than guessed. Replace with something like: "At p. 366 the book prints a summary map of anomaly directions, captioned in Sungenis's own words. The slide is not credited in the book and I could not trace it to a publication; it is not one of the seven figures in Copi, Huterer, Schwarz & Starkman's 2010 review, which the book does cite by name three pages later (p. 369)." Keep the "cites by name three pages later" clause — that is correct, the names appear at p. 369. Rewrite the advocate's premise, which currently has the defender say "that figure is a reproduction of Copi and Starkman's summary of the whole anomaly field"; the defence still works if it says the slide summarises the mainstream's own inventory, without asserting a source we cannot verify.

findings.problem: The entry's central provenance claim — that the source set item 339 aside — is contradicted by the same chapter, and by the entry itself. The refutation says "at the point where he introduces it, the source declines to argue from it" and "The list is running as a proof the one item its own authority set down"; compression.note classifies 339 as `reversed`. But he introduces the hemispheric asymmetry at 7th ed. Vol. I p. 347, twenty-four pages earlier, where he prints the Scientific American/Eriksen block, reproduces a graph labelled "Eriksen &al. ApJ(605)14 (l,b)=(57,10) maximises asymm", and writes: "The significance of Eriksen's finding may go over the heads of most people not familiar with astrophysical language, but the simple interpretation is that all the radiation in the universe, whether it is symmetric or asymmetric, is centered around the Earth." That is arguing from it, in exactly the sense the list uses it. The p. 371 sentence is narrower than the entry makes it: inside a critique of the WMAP nine-year foreground paper, he says power asymmetries are not the cause of the Axis of Evil — a claim about what causes the Axis, not a disavowal of the asymmetry as evidence. Worse, gloss para 5 quotes the p. 347 gloss ("all the radiation in the universe…is centered around the Earth") without noticing it refutes gloss para 1, so the published page contradicts itself.
findings.fix: Reclassify 339. On the strength of p. 347 the list states the source's claim at the source's strength, which is `none` — and saying so costs nothing, because the treatment's real work on 339 is the physics (a posteriori direction, no polarization corroboration), not the drift. Rewrite the refutation clause to what is actually true and still interesting: "He does argue from this anomaly, at p. 347, where he reads Eriksen's asymmetry as showing that 'all the radiation in the universe … is centered around the Earth'. What he declines at p. 371 is narrower — that power asymmetries cause the Axis of Evil — and the list does not distinguish the two." Delete "the one item its own authority set down" and "the one item its own authority set aside" wherever they appear.

findings.problem: The TLDR is stronger than the body it summarises — the pattern both prior sweeps flagged, with the quantifier "All six" doing the damage. "All six of these are real features of the microwave sky and Planck says so — its isotropy paper calls their existence 'uncontested'." I read the Planck sentence in context: it is introduced by an enumeration of the lack of large-angle correlation, low variance, hemispherical asymmetry / dipolar modulation, odd-parity preference, and the large southern temperature decrement. That is four of E02's six items. It does not cover item 331 ("ISW correlations ecliptic-linked") — the body's own ISW paragraph says the literature runs the other way on the ecliptic clause — and it does not cover item 336 ("Cosmic isotropy violations"), which the body answers with "Unknown, and reasonable people are on both sides". Planck's very next clause is that the extent to which these features "provide evidence for a violation of isotropy in the CMB remains unclear", so the TLDR has Planck endorsing the reality of the one item Planck explicitly declines to endorse.
findings.fix: Narrow the quantifier to what the body supports: "Four of these six are real features of the microwave sky and Planck says so — its isotropy paper calls their existence 'uncontested'. The other two are the list's own summary label and a claim about the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect that the ISW literature does not support. What the six do not do is agree with each other." Keep the rest of the TLDR unchanged; the figure-coordinates sentence and the scalar sentence are both correct.

findings.problem: The source's conclusion is characterised as "hedged and disjunctive" by quoting up to the disjunction and stopping there, which is the move the hedge rule exists to forbid — performed on the source instead of by the list. The entry quotes: the CMB's characteristics "suggest that our local system … is either a central source or the central depository or 'sink' for the CMB radiation", and concludes that item 336 "states as established what the source states as a suggestion between disjuncts" (`scope_widened`). The next two sentences on the same page read: "This means that the Earth and its neighbors are in the center of the phenomenon." and, four sentences later, "In either model there can be no other conclusion than the orientation of the CMB is purely geocentric." The disjunction is over the mechanism (source or sink), not over the conclusion, which is stated flatly. The immediately preceding sentence is equally flat: "which combination forms an X and Y axes with Earth directly in the center of it all."
findings.fix: Extend the quoted span through "This means that the Earth and its neighbors are in the center of the phenomenon" and "there can be no other conclusion than the orientation of the CMB is purely geocentric", and drop `scope_widened` for 336 — on this passage the list is not stronger than the source, the source is stronger than the list. If a drift finding is still wanted for 336, it has to rest on something else (e.g. that "cosmic isotropy violations" imports the anomaly literature's technical term for a claim the source makes about a place rather than a field), and that is a `category_shifted` argument, not a hedge-dropping one.

findings.problem: A uniqueness claim about the text we say we searched in full is false in that text. The gloss says "the Cold Spot is present as the figure label above and, in the searched text, nowhere else"; compression.note says "Item 326's Cold Spot appears once, as a coordinate label printed inside a figure … and is not argued from." In the same 7th-edition scan the Cold Spot appears a second time, substantively: he quotes a report that "the result of such collisions would be circular temperature anomalies — similar to the cold spot now seen by Planck", and comments that the Multiverse "will now become modern cosmology's response of choice in order to wiggle out of every piece of evidence that points to a non-Copernican universe" — i.e. he counts the Cold Spot among the evidence being wriggled out of. Separately, the docstring's "Vielva, Cruz and Eridanus return zero occurrences in both texts" is wrong on Cruz: "Cruz &al MNRAS(356)29" is printed on the p. 366 figure itself (OCR'd in the djvu text as "Bele Cruz ri phcnencmeld"). The scoping formula is correctly applied here — the failure is that the scoped claim is false, which is worse than an unscoped one.
findings.fix: Replace both sentences with what the text supports: "In the searched text the Cold Spot appears twice — as a coordinate label on the p. 366 figure, and in a quoted report of a multiverse explanation for it, which he dismisses. Neither place argues a preferred axis from it." That keeps the finding that carries the weight for item 326 and removes the count that a defender can falsify with one search. Correct the Cruz claim in the docstring.

findings.problem: Two printed page numbers are off by one, both inside the compression block, which is the project's headline product. In the archive.org PDF the printed folio is the last line of each page, and the running head at the top carries only the chapter title. On that reading: the "either a central source or the central depository or 'sink'" sentence is on p. 366, not p. 365 — it is on the same page as the figure the entry correctly places at p. 366, four paragraphs above it. And Bennett's item 23, "A deficit in large-scale multipole power exists between the north and south ecliptic hemispheres", is on p. 387, not p. 386. The entry's other four page citations are right: the figure and caption at p. 366, the Bouw footnote at p. 365, the beam-symmetrization block and "power asymmetries are not the cause of the Axis of Evil" at p. 371, and the "fluke" / 99% sentence at p. 367.
findings.fix: Change "(p. 365)" to "(p. 366)" in both compression fields, and "Vol. II ch. 10, p. 386" to "p. 387" in the gloss and docstring. The sources entry's range "Vol. II pp. 386-391" can stay. Note the derivation in the locator so the next reader does not re-litigate it: the folio sits at the foot of the page in this scan, so the djvu text order is [body][footnotes][folio][next page's running head].

findings.problem: "Six directions are printed on it in galactic coordinates" undercounts the figure, and the entry invites the reader to check: "Anyone can redo it in four lines." The page image shows seven labelled directions with coordinates — the six listed plus "SG pole (47,6)", the supergalactic pole. So "Two of the six labels on the figure are nowhere near the cross" is really three of seven. The omission runs against us rhetorically, not for us: (47,6) sits 71 degrees from the Axis of Evil, 63 degrees from the dipole and 38.1 degrees out of the ecliptic plane, so including it strengthens the entry's own point. But a defender who opens the book sees a miscount in the paragraph the entry calls its best evidence.
findings.fix: Say seven, add SG pole (47,6) to the list in the gloss and to the enumeration in refutation paragraph 2, and change "Two of the six labels" to "Three of the seven labelled directions". Add its angles to the refutation's series; they are already computed above.

findings.problem: "Sungenis's reply is not to dispute that" is more generous than the page. The block quote at p. 371 is introduced with "Despite the obvious fudging of the data to fit its Big Bang model, NASA puts on an air of unbiased research as it prides itself on its 'new procedures' in collecting data:", and the sentence immediately after "power asymmetries are not the cause of the Axis of Evil" is "The Axis is caused by the Earth-centered anisotropies in the CMB data, the very anisotropies that NASA is obviously trying to eliminate from the data as much as it can." So he does contest the procedure — he frames it as data manipulation and says the real signal is being scrubbed. The entry quotes "the obvious fudging of the data to fit its Big Bang model" in straw_man without noting that it attaches to this exact passage, so the two blocks are drawing on the same sentences and telling different stories about them.
findings.fix: Replace "is not to dispute that" with the accurate version: "He does not dispute the arithmetic — he disputes the procedure, introducing the WMAP passage as 'the obvious fudging of the data' and following it with the charge that NASA is 'trying to eliminate' the anisotropies. What he does not do is claim the asymmetry as the cause of the Axis." This also removes the appearance that straw_man and the gloss are quoting the same page against each other.

findings.problem: Edition ambiguity on a page citation, which is recurring failure #3 in the sweep notes. The gloss says "The Scientific American paragraph he reproduces at pp. 164-165" with no edition named, in a treatment whose passage, figure, conclusion and every other page number are 7th-edition printed numbers; a reader will take 164-165 for the 7th edition. It is the 2006 printing (the docstring says so, the published gloss does not), and the same block is in the 7th edition at pp. 346-347.
findings.fix: Write "the Scientific American paragraph he reproduces in the 2006 printing at Vol. I pp. 164-165, and again in the seventh edition at pp. 346-347". Citing both is strictly better here, because the 7th-edition location is where the p. 347 'centered around the Earth' gloss sits, which is the material finding #2 turns on.

findings.problem: Two problems in one sentence: "The one place the ISW touches this cluster's central claim, it removes the coincidence rather than supplying one." First, "the one place" is an unscoped universal over an entire literature, of the kind the absence-claim rule targets — the rule's failure mode last sweep was exactly this, constructions the regex does not match sitting in fields it does not read. Second, it is selectively true of the paper being cited. Francis & Peacock's Table 2 does move the quadrupole-octopole alignment probability from 0.09% (ILC) and 1.2% (OT) to 24.5% and 32.9%, and the ecliptic does stop lying along a node line — both correctly reported. But the same paper's Table 3 reports the octopole planarity going the other way, from 17% and 15% to 1.6% and 5.0%, and the paper says in terms: "removal of the estimated local ISW effect seems to make the octopole more planar" and "the planarity of the octopole remains most unusual, and in fact becomes more significant on removal of the ISW signal". A defender who reads the cited paper has that in hand.
findings.fix: Scope the claim and concede the inconvenient half: "In the ISW work located for this entry, the only result bearing on the ecliptic coincidence removes it rather than supplying one — and the same paper is worth reading honestly, because it also finds the octopole's planarity becoming more significant after the local ISW is subtracted, not less. Its own summary is that ~5% significance 'is hardly compelling evidence for any anomaly'." Conceding this costs nothing — octopole planarity is E01's item, not this cluster's — and pre-empts the counter.

findings.problem: Ambiguous antecedent creates a misattribution risk. "A 2022 lensing analysis of the same region put the odds against a large void at about 1:13 to 1:20 relative to plain LambdaCDM. Their own summary is worth quoting … the Cold Spot 'may have a primordial origin rather than being due to line-of-sight effects'." The nearest antecedent for "their own" is the 2022 lensing authors (Owusu, da Silveira Ferreira, Notari & Quartin, arXiv:2211.16139, JCAP 06(2023)040); the quoted sentence is Mackenzie et al. 2017's, two sentences earlier. A reader checking the 2022 paper for it will not find it.
findings.fix: Name the source in the sentence: "Mackenzie's own summary is worth quoting…". Both papers are already in the sources list, so nothing else changes.

findings.problem: The chosen microkelvin figure is the smaller of the two the paper offers, and the paper pairs the larger one with -150 in the same sentence. "-9.1 +/- 6.1 muK" is verbatim Mackenzie et al. for the three-void model and is legitimately their preferred model, but the sentence that puts a number against -150 reads: "even including this void's contribution the total ISW decrement from Table 3 is still only ~-32 muK compared to the ~-150 muK needed to explain the Cold Spot." Quoting -9 against -150 is the more favourable pairing and drops the error bar.
findings.fix: Use the paper's own pairing, which is still decisive and cannot be attacked: "a combined decrement of -9.1 +/- 6.1 muK for their three-void model, and only about -32 muK even counting a fourth void they distrust, against the roughly -150 muK needed."

findings.problem: The same quantity is given two different values in two sections. The steelman says the maximum-asymmetry axis is "62 degrees from the dipole"; the refutation says "63 degrees from the dipole". Recomputed, the separation modulo 180 degrees is 62.74, so 63 is the correct rounding and 62 is a truncation.
findings.fix: Change the steelman's 62 to 63.

findings.problem: The verbatim Planck 2018 VII quotation runs to 79 words, above the 60-word cap for in-copyright quotes (A&A 641, A7 is (c) ESO). The live test only counts words in passage.quote, which here is 54 and compliant, so nothing goes red; the same gap exists elsewhere in the corpus (R02 at 118 words, B04 at 107), so this is a house-wide blind spot rather than an E02 invention, but E02 is the target under review.
findings.fix: Trim to the load-bearing clauses and paraphrase the tail: quote through "…remains unclear. It is plausible that they are indeed simply statistical fluctuations." (44 words) and report the rest in our own words. Worth flagging upward that the cap's test does not read the refutation field.

findings.problem: "those two labels sit 56 and 72 degrees away from the axis the cross is drawn on" — the caption the TLDR just paraphrased names two axes, the dipole axis and the quadrupole/octupole axis, so "the axis" in the singular is loose. Both figures are measured from the Axis of Evil; from the dipole the same two labels are 66 and 63 degrees away.
findings.fix: "…sit 56 and 72 degrees away from the low-multipole arm of that cross".

findings.problem: "Santos and Zhao find that the preferred axis of the parity asymmetry lies close to galactic (270-284 degrees, +50 degrees) — within a few degrees of the CMB dipole". Their masked-map value, (272.3, 49.8), is 5.5 degrees from the dipole at (264, 48), which supports "a few"; but the upper end of the range the entry itself quotes, (284, +50), is 13.2 degrees away. The quoted conclusion about a non-cosmological origin is verbatim and correct.
findings.fix: Either quote the single masked-map value — "(272, +50), about five degrees from the CMB dipole" — or soften to "within five to thirteen degrees of the CMB dipole across their analyses".

findings.field: passage.gloss (finding 1) / refutation opening / steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim / tldr / verdict_challenge.reasoning
findings.problem: The entry's organising claim is that spherical shells and a preferred axis are mutually exclusive evidence — "A sphere centred on you has no axis. An axis has no centre... at most one of these items can be evidence for a central Earth", and in the verdict "the model these items are marshalled for — a central Earth in a spherically symmetric cosmos — predicts no preferred direction at all". The source does not hold a spherically symmetric cosmos. Sungenis's geocentrism is a universe that rotates about a central Earth once a day; that model has a centre AND an axis, and the celestial pole is that axis. Worse, the "[sun-earth]" interpolation Sungenis adds to the quoted sentence shows exactly how he reads the ecliptic result: cosmic structure keyed to our own orbital plane is, for him, further evidence that the Earth is special, not a competing geometry. Shells give centrality, an Earth-keyed axis gives specialness, and the two are consistent as evidence for one conclusion. The advocate block even raises this ("It is a rotation about an axis. An axis is what we claimed") and the preemptive answers a different objection instead — that an unexplained direction is not a claimed centre — leaving the actual hit unanswered. Hutsemekers 2005 itself mentions rotating cosmologies in this connection (astro-ph/0507274, discussion of the mirror-like symmetry: a global rotation "would also induce a rotation of the polarization angles as a function of the distance to the source").
findings.fix: Drop the claim that the two items cannot both be evidence for one conclusion, and keep the weaker, true claim: they are different geometries requiring different physics, and the source welds them with an "in other words" that does no argumentative work. Then answer the axis on its merits, which the entry already does well in IV(a)-(d): the axis does not point at the Earth, it rotates with distance, and its natural frame is the Local Supercluster's, not the Earth's. Recommended replacement for the gloss sentence: "A geocentric cosmos that turns once a day has both a centre and an axis, so these are not formally incompatible; what they are is two unrelated results, resting on different data and different physics, joined by the words 'in other words'." The verdict paragraph's clause "predicts no preferred direction at all" must go with it.

findings.field: passage.gloss (finding 2) / refutation section V / compression.note (third paragraph) / straw_man.detail
findings.problem: The entry's self-declared hardest finding — that Sungenis's ellipsis deletes the CMB so that "the sentence acquires whatever subject the surrounding paragraph supplies — which, on p. 414 of Galileo Was Wrong, is quasars", and that "the claim changes subject from the microwave background to quasars inside a pair of quotation marks" — is materially undercut by the source text. In the Internet Archive OCR of the seventh-edition three-volume scan, the sentence introducing the block quote on printed p. 413 reads: "Lastly, a team studying the orientation of quasars has discovered that they have a preferred axis, the same as they found for radio wavelengths and micro wavelengths (i.e., the CMB)." The book names the microwave background, and glosses "micro wavelengths" as the CMB, one sentence before the quotation. Independently, Urban & Zhitnitsky's own section II.A (arXiv:1011.2425v2, p. 2) says the quasar polarization vectors "tend to identify an axis in the sky which closely align with the direction of the cosmological dipole", and their II.C says the CMB multipole normals point along "the cosmological dipole once again" and the ecliptic — so a single common axis spanning optical, radio and micro is the paper's actual thesis, not something Sungenis manufactured. The mechanical claim is true (the elision does remove the subject of "point", and Sungenis interpolates "[sun-earth]"), but the accusation built on it — that the source is "made to say something about quasars that they said about the microwave background" — is not defensible as written, and it is the first thing a well-informed defender will check. Note also that the entry's IV(d) rebuts an equatorial-frame axis while item 117 claims an ecliptic one; no ecliptic-frame test is reported either way.
findings.fix: Rewrite the finding to what survives: the elision removes the subject of the verb and the interpolation "[sun-earth]" glosses the ecliptic as an Earth-Sun structure, so the compressed item 117 reads as a fact about quasars — but the book itself signposts the CMB one sentence earlier and the cited paper does claim a common axis. Then answer that claim rather than the quotation: the CMB quadrupole/octopole alignment is real and argued at ARG-E01; the quasar A1-A3 axis is near the CMB dipole (astro-ph/0507274 gives the dipole at l=264, b=48 and the quasar axis at l=267, b=69), the 2005 authors call the axis "definitely affected by observational biases", and Urban & Zhitnitsky's own footnote 2 calls the dipole coincidence "mere coincidence" for the purposes of their discussion. Add the strongest form of item 117 to steelman.description and to advocate.best_defense, where it is currently missing.

findings.problem: IV(b) says the handedness flip means "a mirror symmetry about the Galactic plane is a fact about where we sit in the Milky Way... A mechanism tied to the Galaxy, or to the local matter distribution, can produce exactly this". The abstract of the paper cited for the fact says the reverse: "These characteristics make the alignment effect difficult to explain in terms of local mechanisms, namely a contamination by interstellar polarization in our Galaxy" (astro-ph/0507274). The same paper also declines to state the flip as flatly as the entry and the TLDR do: "a counter-clockwise rotation in both the South and North Galactic Caps (S2 symmetry) cannot be totally excluded", "both the slope and the constant of the linear fit depend on the coordinate system", "due to the 180 degree uncertainty, several other complicated or asymmetric solutions to the theta-z relation could be imagined", and the paper explains that a step-like discontinuity at z=0 is expected in general from the way position angles are defined for a structure crossing the observer. The paper's own reading of the mirror symmetry is that it "would be accounted for by a rotation axis close to the A1-A3 axis" — a global rotation, which is nearer the defender's model than ours. advocate.preemptive (b) calls this line "the defender's cleverest move" and instructs that the answer "must not be cut", so the error is pinned in place. It is also load-bearing in the TLDR ("reverses handedness between the galactic hemispheres"), which is where readers meet it first.
findings.fix: Delete "A mechanism tied to the Galaxy, or to the local matter distribution, can produce exactly this; a centre cannot." Replace the paragraph with the hedged version the source supports: the S1 mirror symmetry is the best-defined fit but the paper records that S2 (same handedness in both caps) cannot be totally excluded and that the S1 result depends on the coordinate system through the z=0 discontinuity. Then rest IV on the features that are not coordinate-dependent — the different preferred directions at z~0.5 and z~1.5, the ~30 deg/Gpc rotation, the ~1.5 Gpc alternance, and the observational-bias passage. Soften the TLDR clause to "whose preferred direction rotates about 30 degrees per gigaparsec" and drop the handedness clause, since it cannot carry TLDR weight.

findings.field: tldr / refutation section I / compression.note (link one)
findings.problem: The TLDR says Varshni's "conclusion was that if quasar redshifts are cosmological you get an absurdity, so they are not cosmological", and section I says item 90 asserts "the horn of a dilemma that the man who drew the dilemma rejected, in print, in the same paragraph". Varshni did not reject it and did not conclude that. His closing sentences (Ap&SS 43:8) are: "We are essentially left with only one possibility - No. 3 in the cosmological red-shift interpretation. However, before we accept such an unaesthetic possibility, we must raise the question: Are the 'red shifts' real? We wish to point out that we have proposed an alternative explanation..." That is a deferral plus a pointer to his own model, not a rejection. The book's footnote 512 characterises it more accurately than we do: "Although Varshni was firm on his discovery, he did leave room for an alternative explanation." On a project whose thesis is that compression hardens hedges, publishing our own hardening of the primary source's hedge in the headline field is the specific thing a defender will quote back.
findings.fix: TLDR: "...his own paper treats it as a cost of the redshift hypothesis, not a discovery — he calls the geocentric horn 'unaesthetic', asks whether the redshifts are real at all, and points at his own model, which 'does not require any red shifts'". Section I: replace "rejected, in print, in the same paragraph" with "declined to accept, in print, in the same paragraph, in favour of doubting the redshifts". compression.note already says "declines", which is fine; leave it.

findings.problem: The entry states that the book's "quasar distribution problem" sentence carries a reference: "the reference given is to Varshni's paper rather than to anyone using the phrase." In the OCR of the scan cited, that sentence (printed p. 405: "Soon after Varshni's work, astronomers found over 20,000 quasars, and none of them altered Varshni's original results. In fact, they refer to it as the 'quasar distribution problem.'") carries no footnote marker at all, and the footnote numbering runs continuously from 513 on p. 404 to 514 on p. 406 with nothing in between. So no reference is given. The entry's own docstring warns that superscripts in this scan are OCR-degraded to degree signs and that footnote numbers must not be cited from it — which is exactly the evidence class this claim rests on. The true state of affairs is stronger for us than what we published.
findings.fix: "...a phrase presented as the field's own name for a result it finds awkward; no source is given for the phrase anywhere on the page, in the text of that scan as searched." Same paragraph could add the neighbouring unsourced claim, which is checkable and false: "astronomers found over 20,000 quasars, and none of them altered Varshni's original results."

findings.problem: "Shells drawn from 384 objects that were consistent with chance in 1976 have not been recovered from a catalogue three orders of magnitude larger." This is an unscoped absence claim of exactly the banned shape — it asserts that nothing in the literature or in DR16Q recovers the shells, which is a claim about a corpus made from no search, and it implies someone looked. The ratcheting test does not catch it because the construction ("have not been recovered") is outside the regex, which is the migration failure the curmudgeon file predicts. Everywhere else in this entry the discipline is exemplary — the item-322 search log is scoped correctly and the section VI ecliptic claim is scoped to "the abstracts and stated conclusions of the four papers cited in this section" — so this is the one lapse.
findings.fix: "No recovery of Varshni's shells from a modern catalogue is reported in the DR16Q catalogue paper or in any of the quasar-clustering papers cited on this page; we did not locate one. Not-located is not not-existing, and the point that carries the section is the arithmetic above, not the search."

findings.problem: The gloss states as established fact: "The same page 413 paragraph is where ARG-E13 traced item 194, so items 194 and 321 descend from one page of one chapter." ARG-E13 does not say that. /home/claude/spinning-ball-review/scripts/_b7_E13.py records item 194 as "probably Volume I, ch. 3, pp. 413-415", explicitly "Held loosely", and adds that "194 may simply be a duplicate of item 321 filed into the wrong cluster"; its compression note says "item 194 probably does". Publishing E13's hedged attribution as a settled derivation is a cross-claim consistency defect on the one axis the README says is the product — "Does every claimed derivation survive following the chain backwards" — and a critic can put the two pages side by side.
findings.fix: "ARG-E13 provisionally traced item 194 to this same passage (pp. 413-415), holding the attribution loosely and noting that 194 may be a duplicate of item 321 filed into the wrong cluster; on the reading here that provisional attribution stands." Do not upgrade E13's hedge from this file.

findings.field: clusters.py E04 note (renders next to the verdict chip); not reported in the module docstring
findings.problem: scripts/clusters.py line 562ff gives E04 the note "Real, replicated signals with an accepted astrophysical mechanism — black-hole spins align with the filaments they sit in." The treatment says the opposite and says it repeatedly: "not fully explained", "The effect is real, replicated and not fully explained, and this page says so without hedging", and advocate.preemptive closes with "One thing this entry must never do is describe the quasar polarization alignment as explained or as a known systematic. It is neither." The cluster note renders into the summary line read by people who never expand the entry, so the page contradicts itself in the two places a skim-reader sees. This is recurring failure 5 from review/curmudgeon.md, which hit five of twelve batch-8 targets. The docstring reports clusters.py's null originator/work/year and the real_source omission of Varshni 1976, but not this.
findings.fix: Report the note upward with the other clusters.py fields. Proposed replacement: "Real, replicated signals. The mechanism on the table — quasar spin axes aligning with the filaments they grew in — covers alignment relative to a structure but not the gigaparsec coherence, which remains unexplained. Preferred directions differ by redshift slice, and Nadathur 2013 showed Clowes's algorithm finds Gpc 'structures' in explicitly homogeneous random simulations." The cluster note's "and hemisphere" clause should go for the same reason as finding 3.

findings.problem: "The list inherited both and files them four items apart (item 90 and item 117)". Items 90 and 117 are 27 items apart in the specimen corpus (scripts/corpus.py, scripts/assign.py). E04's four items are 90, 117, 321 and 322.

findings.problem: Pelgrims 2019 is reported as "concluding that thermal dust 'cannot fully account for the reported quasar optical polarization alignments'" and "found dust cannot fully account for it". The abstract of arXiv:1709.10271 (A&A 622:A145) reads "We further found arguments suggesting that Galactic thermal dust cannot fully account for...". findings.field: refutation section II / module docstring item 5
findings.problem: The clump statistic is not reproducible from what is published. Re-running with numpy default_rng(20260809), 4000 realisations, 384 draws on [0.2, 3.53], I reproduce the fixed-bin figures exactly (37.9 +/- 4.9 against the published 37.8 +/- 4.9; beta(2,3) 48.4 +/- 5.2 against 48.4 +/- 5.1) but get 62.7 +/- 5.2 and 73.2 +/- 5.2 for the clump counts against the published 64.1 +/- 5.3 and 76.7 +/- 5.3. "Clumps of two or more objects lying within 0.002 of each other" is ambiguous between single-linkage chaining and pairwise proximity, and the RNG is not named. The README's sourcing standard is "a public source or a reproducible calculation".
findings.fix: State the linkage rule and the generator in the docstring — e.g. "maximal runs of sorted redshifts with consecutive gaps <= 0.002, numpy default_rng" — or ship the eight-line script alongside the entry.

findings.problem: Friday, Clowes & Williger 2022 are quoted as reporting an alignment "at least an order of magnitude larger than any so far observed". The abstract of arXiv:2201.11474 continues "...with the exception of quasar-polarisation / radio-jet alignment", and the exception is the very effect the same steelman paragraph is discussing.
findings.fix: Add the exception clause, or end the quotation before the comparative claim.

findings.problem: The TLDR asserts that "every independent re-analysis since 2008 ... finds the sky consistent with isotropy." Refutation section seven says the opposite in its own words: "One research programme continues to report the asymmetry. Lior Shamir has published it from SDSS, Pan-STARRS, DES, HST, HSC and JWST deep fields, in refereed venues through 2024-25 ... That exchange is unresolved and this page is not adjudicating it." Shamir's 2024 reply (arXiv:2404.13864, verified) is in part a re-analysis of the same public catalogues, and PASA 41:e038 is refereed. This is recurring failure 2/6 verbatim - the TLDR is stronger than the body it summarises, and the universal quantifier is the load-bearing word. It also breaks the restraint rule the entry's own docstring invokes at point 6 ("E01's restraint rule applies: represent the open part as open"). Highest reader impact of anything here, because the TLDR is what a skimmer takes away.
findings.fix: Replace "every independent re-analysis since 2008 ... finds the sky consistent with isotropy" with a scoped version plus the concession, e.g. "and every re-analysis of Longo's and Shamir's own catalogues by other groups - Galaxy Zoo 2008, Hayes 2017, Iye 2021, Patel & Desmond 2024 - has come back consistent with isotropy, though the group that reports the asymmetry is still publishing and that exchange is open." Keep the 4.0-to-0.29 sigma clause; it is accurate.

findings.problem: Both fields set "the preprint's 'signal exceeding 5 sigma'" against "the peer-reviewed version's axis-free number ... 7.9 x 10^-4, about 3.2 sigma", and the compression note files this under the heading "Link one, Longo to the book: qualifiers removed at the sentence level" as drift evidence. The refereed paper carries the 5 sigma figure too. PLB 699:224 states in its own section 3: "Overall the asymmetry is -0.0607 +/- 0.0118, a 5.15 sigma effect with a probability of 2.5x10^-7 for occurring by chance", and its Table I prints the same numbers (verified in the arXiv:1104.2815 full text, which is the published version). The book therefore quoted a figure that survives intact into the journal article - it dropped no qualifier here, and charging it with one is unfair to the source in a block whose entire purpose is fairness to the source. Each clause is literally true, which is what makes it worse: a defender opens the paper we cite, finds 5.15 sigma on page 8, and concludes we implied a walk-back that never happened. Related arithmetic error in refutation section seven's verdict paragraph: "the significance halves when the axis is not assumed" - 5.15 to 3.16 is a 39% reduction, and in probability it is a factor of 3,000.
findings.fix: Recast as the within-paper contrast, which is real and survives inspection: in PLB 699:224 the sector analysis over pre-chosen right-ascension ranges (165-225 deg and 15 +/- 30 deg, carried over from the earlier study) gives 5.15 sigma, while the unbinned dipole fit that "made no prior assumptions for the dipole axis", after the look-elsewhere penalty computed over 100 randomly chosen axes, gives 7.9 x 10^-4, about 3.2 sigma - and the same axis-free fit in the 2009 preprint, before that penalty, gave 1.51 x 10^-4. Drop the 5 sigma line from the list of hedge-drop evidence entirely; the truncated 1.6 sigma quotation carries the drift finding on its own and is fully verified. Replace "the significance halves" with "the significance drops from 5.15 sigma to about 3.2 sigma".

findings.problem: "The book cites the 2009 preprint and dates it 2009 while printing the 2007 title and a bare DOI stub; the reader who follows the citation lands on a different version of the paper from the one the title names." This does not describe either of the book's actual citations. arXiv:0707.3793 and arXiv:0904.2529 carry the identical title "Evidence for a Preferred Handedness of Spiral Galaxies" (verified on both abs pages; the entry's own sources block assigns that same title to both), so "the 2007 title" identifies nothing and cannot name a different version. What the scan actually shows is two different and better defects. The footnote on Vol. I p. 384 (leaf 397) gives the URL "http://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/0707/0707.3793.pdf, p. 9" and then quotes the abstract of the 2009 paper ("The new study uses 15,158 with redshifts <0.085 ... a signal exceeding 5 sigma"), before adding "In a slightly different version of the same article" with the 0904.2529 URL. The footnote at pp. 240 and 448 (leaves 253, 461) reads: "'Evidence for a Preferred Handedness of Spiral Galaxies,' Michael Longo, Physics Letters B 10.1016, 2009; http://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/0904/0904.2529.pdf" - a preprint title and a truncated DOI attached to a Physics Letters B article that is titled "Detection of a Dipole in the Handedness of Spiral Galaxies with Redshifts z ~ 0.04" and appeared in 2011. On a provenance project this is the wrong sentence to get wrong, and the true version is the stronger one.
findings.fix: Replace with what the scan shows: "The book's citations do not resolve to one document. The footnote at p. 384 quotes the 2009 preprint's abstract under a URL for the 2007 preprint, then flags the next quotation as coming from 'a slightly different version of the same article'. The footnote at pp. 240 and 448 attaches the preprint's title, a truncated DOI ('Physics Letters B 10.1016') and the year 2009 to a journal article that appeared in Physics Letters B in 2011 under a different title. A reader following either citation lands on a preprint, not on the paper named."

findings.problem: "Three of the thirty clusters recorded as untraced have now been audited and all three came back with a source, so the untraced count should still be read as an upper bound in one direction only." Both halves are wrong against our own published records. Four have been audited, and two of the four returned no source: E17 carries compression assessed='no_source' with the note "There is no original to hold this against ... no named originator, no cited publication" (deep.py lines 335-347), and C08 carries assessed='no_source' with a documented search log (scripts/_b8_C08.py lines 8-50, "The search was run and it TERMINATED IN A RESULT ... pre_modern was CONSIDERED AND REJECTED"). E13 and E05 are the two that came back with a source. The conclusion drawn from the false premise also contradicts README.md line 118 ("treat the remaining 28 as provisional in both directions") and _b7_E13.py's own gloss.
findings.fix: "Four of the thirty clusters recorded as untraced have now been audited and the answers have split two and two: E13 and E05 came back with a documented ancestor in Galileo Was Wrong, E17 and C08 came back with no original to compare against. The count is provisional in both directions."

findings.problem: The published audit trail for the item-323 absence claim does not reproduce. The note says the full-text search for "radio galax" in the seventh-edition scan "returns Singal's radio source counts (Vol. I, p. 388) and the Nodland-Ralston polarization-rotation discussion (Vol. II, pp. 380-381)". Running that search over the same item's OCR: "Singal" occurs exactly once in all three volumes, on printed Vol. I p. 416 (leaf 429), in the section quoting "Peculiar motion of the solar system ... a violation of the Copernican principle in radio sky". Printed Vol. I p. 388 (leaf 401) is a different section - "Distant Radio Sources Confirm Non-Copernican Universe", on J. C. Jackson of Northumbria University, 2012. The Nodland-Ralston locator at Vol. II pp. 380-381 does check out (leaves 1186-1187, Chapter 10). The absence conclusion for item 323 is unaffected and I could not locate a radio-galaxy handedness claim either, but the whole value of a scoped absence claim is that a reader can redo the search, and this one sends them to the wrong page and the wrong author. Same defect in the module docstring, lines 72-79.
findings.fix: "...which returns Singal's radio-source anisotropy at Vol. I p. 416 and J. C. Jackson's distant-radio-sources section at Vol. I p. 388, together with the Nodland-Ralston polarization-rotation discussion at Vol. II pp. 380-381 - the last of which belongs to ARG-E13, and none of which is a handedness claim."

findings.problem: "Shamir's own leading candidate explanation is a Doppler-brightening selection effect." In arXiv:2502.18781 he does not rank it. Section 5 gives two alternatives in order - 5.1 "Anomaly in the LSS" (the early universe was more homogeneous in spin directions, with the axis near the Galactic pole a coincidence) and 5.2 "Physics of galaxy rotation" (the Doppler reading, introduced as "another explanation could be") - and the abstract puts the structural reading first: "The reason for the difference may be related to the structure of the early Universe, but it can also be related to the physics of galaxy rotation." He then argues against the Doppler reading himself: "This explanation is challenged by the fact that the effect of the rotational velocity have merely a mild impact on the brightness of galaxies, and therefore is not expected to lead to the dramatic difference of ~50%." The entry reports that objection two sentences later, so the page half-contradicts its own characterisation. Attributing a preference to a living author that his paper does not state is the kind of thing this project is supposed to be strict about.
findings.fix: "Shamir offers two readings of his own result, and the second is a Doppler-brightening selection effect ..." The rest of the paragraph, including the "should peak at around the Galactic pole" quotation and his own too-small objection, is verified verbatim and needs no change.

findings.problem: Two problems in the same paragraph, both in the sentence "the two things this axis is nearest are the spin axis of our own Galaxy and the middle of the patch of sky the survey happened to cover". (a) Those are one direction, not two. The north Galactic pole is at (192.86 deg, 27.13 deg) and the SDSS DR6 northern-cap centre Longo prints is (192 deg, 27 deg) - 0.8 deg apart. Listing 21.5 deg and 22.3 deg as separate near-coincidences reads as padding to anyone who checks, and invites the reply that the survey covers the northern Galactic cap by construction so the two can never be separated by this data. (b) The 21.5 deg figure is not ours. Longo prints it on p. 11 of PLB 699:224 - "This axis is 21.5 deg away from the north pole of our galaxy (NGP in Fig. 2) at b=90 deg" - and answers it in the next sentence: "our galaxy has its spin vector generally aligned with the preferred axis of spiral galaxies, corresponding to a probability for this to occur by chance of (1-cos 21.5 deg)/2 = 3.5%." The entry says "Recomputed here by spherical cosine rule" and never mentions that the author anticipated the objection and has a published reply to it.
findings.fix: Say the two are one direction: "the axis sits 21.5 deg from the north Galactic pole, and the centre of the SDSS DR6 northern cap that Longo prints - (192 deg, 27 deg) - is the same direction to within a degree, so on this survey the Galaxy's spin axis and the middle of the observed patch cannot be told apart." And credit Longo with the number and his answer: he reads the 21.5 deg as our Galaxy being aligned with the cosmic axis at a 3.5% chance level, which is a coherent reading and still fixes only a direction, not a place.

findings.problem: "Iye, Yagi & Fukumoto devoted an entire paper (Spin Parity of Spiral Galaxies I, 2019) to confirming that relationship against 146 galaxies." The author list belongs to a different paper in the series. Paper I is Iye, M., Tadaki, K. and Fukumoto, H. 2019, ApJ 886, 133 - cited in exactly that form in the reference lists of both arXiv:2011.00662 (line 438) and arXiv:2605.05570 (line 604). Iye, Yagi & Fukumoto is Paper III, ApJ 907, 123, which the entry already cites correctly in its sources block; the two have been crossed. The substance is right: Paper III's introduction confirms "a sample of 146 spiral galaxies that all spiral structure in these galaxies is indeed 'trailing'".
findings.fix: "Iye, Tadaki & Fukumoto devoted an entire paper (Spin Parity of Spiral Galaxies I, ApJ 886:133, 2019) to confirming that relationship against 146 galaxies with independent distance and velocity information."

findings.problem: work="WRK-SUNGENIS-2006" renders through render.py's wlink() as "Galileo Was Wrong: The Church Was Right (2006)" immediately above a locator and quotation that the entry itself dates to the seventh edition of 2013 - and this is the one entry in the corpus that proves the material cannot be in the 2006 printing, having searched its OCR and found zero hits for "Longo". The passage header therefore carries a date the gloss three paragraphs later refutes. This is recurring failures 3 and 5 in combination (edition dating; a record that renders into the entry and contradicts it). The locator does disclose the edition, which limits the damage, and E04, E08, E09, E12, E14 and others share the same work id, so the fix belongs to works.py rather than to this file.
findings.fix: Integrator-side: add a WRK-SUNGENIS-2013 record for the seventh edition (the existing imprint field already documents it: "three volumes from the sixth edition of January 2013 ... 7th ed. 2013") and point E05 and the other seventh-edition-sourced entries at it. If that is out of scope for this batch, record it in review/corrections.json rather than leaving the 2006 chip standing unexplained.

findings.problem: Both paragraphs are written so that they become false the moment the integrator applies the fix they report. The gloss says "Our cluster record for E05 carries no originator, no work and no year ... clusters.py is owned by the integrator and was not edited from here; the finding is reported rather than applied", and the compression note repeats "Our cluster record carries no originator, no work and no year for E05." Both are accurate today (clusters.py line 567 has originator=None, originator_work=None, year=None). Once the reported edit lands, the published page will be telling readers something about itself that stopped being true - the exact mechanism of recurring failure 4, and the reason the rule says to write about our own record in the past tense after the fix lands. E13 shipped with the same coupling, so this is the pattern repeating rather than a one-off.
findings.fix: Either have the integrator apply the clusters.py change and rewrite both paragraphs in the past tense ("Our cluster record carried no originator until this audit; the ancestor is Galileo Was Wrong, 7th ed., Vol. I, pp. 383-387"), or cut the self-description from the prose and put it in review/corrections.json. Anchor any clusters.py edit on the cluster key "E05", never on the originator= line.

findings.problem: "published in Physics Letters B, and never retracted" is an unscoped absence claim about the whole publication record, made from no stated search. It is the banned construction; it slips past the ratchet only because the regex covers "never mentions/cites/uses/wrote/says/appears/treats" and not "never retracted", which is precisely the migration the test's own comment predicts ("writers have learned the regex, not the rule").
findings.fix: Scope it or drop it: "published in Physics Letters B in 2011, with no retraction or corrigendum recorded against it on the journal's article page as of this review" - or simply end the sentence at "published in Physics Letters B", which loses nothing.

findings.problem: "The book says as much elsewhere on the page - 'the universe spins around its center of mass in only one direction'." That sentence is on printed Vol. I p. 384 (leaf 397), two pages before the p. 386 passage under discussion, and it continues "(clockwise), and does so with a slight precession". "Elsewhere on the page" is wrong about the page.
findings.fix: "The book says as much two pages earlier - 'the universe spins around its center of mass in only one direction (clockwise)' (p. 384)."

findings.problem: "Neither is the plane of the equinoxes on either reading of the phrase, and 23.5 degrees is not the separation from anything here." 23.44 degrees is exactly the separation between the two poles named in the preceding sentence - the north celestial pole and the north ecliptic pole - so as written the clause hands a pedantic defender a free correction in a paragraph whose whole authority is arithmetic.
findings.fix: "...and 23.5 degrees is not the separation between Longo's axis and any of them; it is the separation between the celestial and ecliptic poles, which is the one place the book's number could have come from."

findings.field: tldr (and refutation section 5 heading, steelman KERNEL)
findings.problem: The TLDR asserts a uniqueness that the current literature falsifies: "The one genuinely Earth-facing fact is that Andromeda's plane is seen edge-on from here", echoed by section 5's "The one fact that does involve us". Kanehisa, Pawlowski & Libeskind, "Andromeda's asymmetric satellite system as a challenge to cold dark matter cosmology", Nature Astronomy, published 11 April 2025, report a second and stronger Milky-Way-referenced fact: "All but one of Andromeda's 37 satellite galaxies are contained within 107 degrees of our Galaxy", a 4.7-sigma departure from isotropy found in "less than 0.3% (0.5% when accounting for possible observational incompleteness) of Andromeda-like systems", and described in the abstract as "aligned towards the Milky Way". It is by the same Pawlowski group whose 2013 "fortunate" line the entry leans on, it postdates every source cited except the two 2026 preprints, and section 5's selection-effect answer does not touch it — the asymmetry is azimuthal about the MW direction, not an orientation-detectability effect, and the authors explicitly tested observational incompleteness. This is the strongest form of the argument as of 2026 and the steelman does not reach it, so the KERNEL tier is not actually met. The substantive answer is straightforward and strengthens the entry: it is an alignment toward a galaxy 780 kpc away, unchanged if the Sun sat anywhere in the disc, and it is a claim about M31's satellite distribution rather than about the Earth.
findings.fix: Drop the uniqueness in both places — TLDR to "The Earth-facing facts on offer are that Andromeda's plane is seen edge-on from here and that its satellites are lopsided towards our Galaxy", section 5 heading to "The facts that do involve our line of sight, stated at full strength and then answered." Add Kanehisa/Pawlowski/Libeskind 2025 to the KERNEL and to section 5 with the 107-degree, 4.7-sigma and <0.3% figures, and answer it on the same ground section 4 already occupies: the referent is M31 and the MW, two galaxies, and the configuration is invariant under moving the Sun anywhere in the Galactic disc. Add the source: Nature Astronomy (2025), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-025-02480-3.

findings.field: untraceable (paragraph 2, "The geocentric compendium ... was searched in full")
findings.problem: The published search log states: "'Kroupa', 'Ibata', 'M31', 'Tully', 'plane of satellites' and 'disk of satellites' each return zero hits in that text." Tully does not return zero. I re-downloaded the identical artifact — the same Internet Archive item, 5,499,250 bytes and 134,983 lines, matching the fingerprint the entry itself publishes — and "Tully" returns 2 case-insensitive hits. One is substantive: "Next, galaxies in the Fisher-Tully catalogue that showed large amounts of rotation and interval motion (the opposite extreme from the dwarf irregulars) were studied", which sits inside the very redshift-quantization passage the entry assigns to ARG-E12 in the next sentence. The other is OCR noise in a scanned magazine page. The conclusion is unaffected — the Fisher-Tully catalogue is not the satellite-plane literature — but this is the one paragraph written to be checked by a reader with a grep, and it fails on the first try. Kroupa (0), Ibata (0), M31 (0), "plane of satellites" (0) and "disk of satellites" (0) all confirmed correct.
findings.fix: Move Tully out of the zero-hit list and into the E12 sentence: "'Kroupa', 'Ibata', 'M31', 'plane of satellites' and 'disk of satellites' each return zero hits in that text. 'Tully' returns two, one of them OCR noise and the other the Fisher-Tully catalogue inside the redshift-quantization passage that belongs to ARG-E12." This costs nothing and makes the paragraph survive the check it invites.

findings.field: clusters.py E06 note (renders via render.py:180 as the summary line under the verdict chip)
findings.problem: The cluster record reads "A real LambdaCDM tension that has substantially deflated; with Gaia proper motions the Milky Way plane looks transient rather than rotation-supported." render.py line 180 emits a["basis"] — which build.py sets from the cluster note — as the ks-tldr paragraph immediately under the verdict chip, so it is read before anything is expanded. The treatment's section 1 argues the direct opposite at length and with citations: Seo et al. 2024 still get 0.00-3.40%, the Cen A follow-up is titled "remains a challenge", and Sawala's own 2026 follow-up reconciles rather than closes. The published page therefore tells a skim reader the tension has deflated and tells an expanding reader it has not. The agent recorded this in the docstring and correctly kept it out of the prose (no future-tense self-criticism, which is right), but recording is not applying — this is the "recorded, NOT ACTUALLY APPLIED" pattern curmudgeon.md names as the highest-leverage item on the list, now on its fifth occurrence.
findings.fix: Edit clusters.py anchored on the "E06" key, never on the originator= line: replace the note with "A real and still-unresolved LambdaCDM tension. Sawala et al. 2023 answered the Milky Way case and said so; Seo et al. 2024 rebuilt the rarity test and still get 0.00-3.40%, and the Centaurus A result of 2021 is titled 'remains a challenge'. No geocentric content either way." Then re-run tests/run.sh, since the basis string renders into the page.

findings.problem: "Dwarf" returns 9 case-insensitive occurrences in that text, not twelve — verified against the byte-identical artifact. The itemisation is also incomplete: the entry accounts for "Gulliver, a simile about Hubble, and the phrase 'dwarfs any other'", which covers hits 1-5, and the astronomical run is hits 6-8 (the dwarf-irregular redshift-quantization passage, correctly identified). The ninth is unaccounted for — a geocentric passage about the firmament, "since it dwarfs the rest of the universe in comparison". Same failure class as the Tully hit and in the same sentence: a published count a reader can check in one command.
findings.fix: "'Dwarf' returns nine, of which one run is astronomical — the dwarf-irregular redshift-quantization passage, which is ARG-E12's material and a different argument — and the rest are Gulliver, a simile about Hubble, and two uses of 'dwarfs' meaning 'is much larger than'."

findings.field: tldr ("their own 2026 mock-observation study finds that orientation is one of the two a survey can detect at all")
findings.problem: This hardens the cited result into a binary the paper does not state. Crosby, Pawlowski, Muller & Jerjen (arXiv:2602.20447) say: "Satellite planes that are viewed nearly edge-on or face-on, are the most readily detected. In contrast, intermediate orientations and systems with fewer satellites yield low detection success rates." Low is not zero, and "most readily detected" is a rate statement, not a claim that only two orientations are detectable at all. The body is closer but still hardens it — section 5 says intermediate orientations "are missed", where the steelman's "largely missed" is the accurate version. This is precisely the pattern both sweeps flagged: the TLDR written from memory of the argument comes out stronger than the body, which is itself stronger than the source.
findings.fix: TLDR: "...and their own 2026 mock-observation study finds that edge-on and face-on are the orientations a survey most readily detects, with intermediate ones largely missed." Section 5: change "while intermediate orientations are missed" to "while intermediate orientations yield low detection rates", which is the paper's own phrasing.

findings.field: tldr ("its discoverers call that orientation fortunate" / "their own 2026 mock-observation study")
findings.problem: Both attributions point at "its discoverers", whose antecedent in the sentence is Andromeda's plane — that is Ibata et al. 2013 (Nature 493:62, sixteen authors) and Conn et al. 2013. The word "fortunate" is Pawlowski, Kroupa & Jerjen 2013 (MNRAS 435:1928), and the 2026 mock-observation paper is Crosby, Pawlowski, Muller & Jerjen. There is no author overlap between Ibata et al. 2013 and either of those. The body gets this right — it names Pawlowski, Kroupa & Jerjen explicitly in section 5 and in the steelman — so the defect is confined to the TLDR, which is where readers who never expand will take it. On a project whose product is provenance, a misattributed quotation in the headline is expensive out of proportion to its size.
findings.fix: "...which is the condition for detecting its rotation at all: Pawlowski, Kroupa and Jerjen call that orientation fortunate, and a 2026 mock-observation study from the same group finds edge-on and face-on are the orientations a survey most readily detects."

findings.field: straw_man.detail ("Nobody in the field expects satellite galaxies to be isotropically distributed")
findings.problem: Two of the entry's own cited papers say the opposite in their abstracts. Muller et al. 2018 (Science 359:534, which the sources list quotes for the <0.5% figure): "Cosmological simulations predict that most satellite galaxy systems are close to isotropic with random motions." Kanehisa et al. 2025 (Nature Astronomy): "The standard model of cosmology predicts that most satellite galaxy systems are near-isotropic." A defender needs one line to quote our own source list back at us. The next sentence of our own paragraph already states the defensible version — that the dispute is over degree, since filament accretion and group infall produce some anisotropy in ordinary simulations — so the opening sentence is an overstatement the paragraph itself walks back.
findings.fix: Replace the opening clause with the qualified version: "Nobody in the field expects perfect isotropy — accretion along filaments, infall in groups, and the Magellanic system arriving as a pair all produce some anisotropy in ordinary simulations. What the simulations predict is a near-isotropic distribution with random motions, and the dispute is over degree: whether the observed systems are thinner and more coherent than the simulations manage."

findings.problem: The field labels the quotation as "Ibata et al., Nature 493:62 (2013), on the Andromeda plane: 'it has been claimed that the apparently planar distribution of satellites is not predicted within standard cosmology ... However, other studies dispute this conclusion.'" In the abstract that sentence is not about the Andromeda plane. It closes the paragraph about the MILKY WAY's satellites — "An early analysis noted that dwarf galaxies may not be isotropically distributed around our Galaxy ... These suspicions are supported by recent analyses, and it has been claimed that..." — and the Andromeda plane is only reported in the following sentence, "Here we report the existence (99.998% significance)...". The substantive point the compression note draws from it survives intact (Ibata et al. print the dispute inside their own abstract, and that hedge is gone by the time the item is three words long), but the label attaches the hedge to the wrong claim, inside the field whose entire job is the faithful side-by-side.
findings.fix: Relabel: "Ibata et al., Nature 493:62 (2013), whose abstract prints the dispute over the Milky Way satellite plane before reporting the Andromeda one: '...' And on the Andromeda alignment itself: '...'" No change to the quoted text or to the note.

findings.field: compression.note ("adds a word the satellite-plane literature does not use")
findings.problem: This is an unscoped absence claim about an entire literature, in a field that renders to the reader. It survives the ratchet in tests/test_provenance.py only because the word "searched" appears in the following clause and lands inside the +/-160-character _SCOPE window — the exact mechanism curmudgeon.md describes when it says writers have learned the regex rather than the rule, and notes that a green ratchet is evidence about the fields it reads and nothing more. The underlying fact is fine and I checked it: "ecliptic" returns zero in Pawlowski, Pflamm-Altenburg & Kroupa 2012, zero in Pawlowski, Kroupa & Jerjen 2013 and zero in Sawala et al. 2023. The claim just needs to say that instead of generalising over a literature nobody sampled.
findings.fix: "'Cluster axes ecliptic' adds a word that is not located in any of the three satellite-plane papers searched for this entry — Pawlowski, Pflamm-Altenburg & Kroupa 2012, Pawlowski, Kroupa & Jerjen 2013 and Sawala et al. 2023, in which 'ecliptic' returns zero — and no measurement tying cluster axes to the ecliptic was located in the papers searched."

findings.field: untraceable (paragraph 3, "Where the vocabulary of item 330 does live")
findings.problem: "'Ecliptic' is dense in that same scan — scores of occurrences — but all of the ones read here are in the microwave-background chapter." The scoping ("read here") is compliant with the house rule, so this is not a rule violation, but the sample is unrepresentative in a way that weakens the inference the paragraph draws. There are 146 occurrences in that text, and sampling them at a fixed stride turns up several that are plainly not CMB material: the obliquity of the ecliptic in the ancient-cosmology chapter; the Miller ether-drift direction ("towards Draco near the northern pole of the ecliptic (17 hours RA, Dec +68)"), which is a different argument on the same list; and a passage explaining the seasons by "the swaying movement of the ecliptic". A defender can say we read the hits that suited the conclusion. The Miller passage in particular is a non-CMB astronomical use of the word inside the same volume.
findings.fix: Say what was sampled and acknowledge the spread: "'Ecliptic' is dense in that same scan — 146 occurrences — and the ones sampled for this entry fall into three groups: the microwave-background chapter arguing that the CMB multipoles line up with the Earth's orbital plane (ARG-E01's claim, in ARG-E01's words), the Miller ether-drift discussion, and incidental uses for the obliquity and the seasons. None of the sampled occurrences attaches the word to galaxy-cluster axes, and the sentence that would license item 330 was not located in the text searched."

findings.field: clusters.py E06 real_source (carried into data/ via build.py lines 140 and 158)
findings.problem: real_source is "Sawala et al. 2023, Nature Astronomy 7:481" and nothing else, so the record names the paper that argues the anomaly away as the source of items that assert the anomaly. The papers the three items actually compress are Kroupa, Theis & Boily 2005, Kroupa et al. 2010, Pawlowski, Pflamm-Altenburg & Kroupa 2012, Ibata et al. 2013 and Muller et al. 2018 — all five of which the treatment cites. This does not render in the argument body for entries that have a deep treatment (render.py only emits real_source_cited on the cluster-depth path), but build.py carries it into the published dataset as real_source_cited, where it is the machine-readable answer to the question this project exists to answer. Reported in the docstring, not applied.
findings.fix: clusters.py, anchored on the "E06" key: real_source="Kroupa, Theis & Boily 2005, A&A 431:517; Pawlowski, Pflamm-Altenburg & Kroupa 2012, MNRAS 423:1109; Ibata et al. 2013, Nature 493:62; Muller et al. 2018, Science 359:534; critique in Sawala et al. 2023, Nature Astronomy 7:481".

findings.field: untraceable (paragraph 2, "'Andromeda' returns two, both of them an Italian publisher's address in the bibliography")
findings.problem: Both hits are the same Italian publisher — "Societa Editrice Andromeda, via S. Allendel, 40139" — but only one is in the bibliography. The other is in the running text, in the passage on Bartocci's book about Einstein and Olinto De Pretto. The characterisation is right; the location is half wrong.
findings.fix: "'Andromeda' returns two, both of them the same Italian publisher's name — once in the running text on Bartocci's De Pretto book, once in the bibliography entry for it."

findings.field: tldr ("every structure in it is referenced to other galaxies rather than to us")
findings.problem: The Milky Way's satellite plane is referenced to our own Galaxy, not to another one. The body is careful about exactly this — section 4 says the structure "is fitted in galactocentric coordinates" and the steelman's rebuttal says "the body all three sentences are referenced to is a galaxy" — so the TLDR is the only place the claim overreaches. A defender gets a cheap correction out of it in the first sentence they read.
findings.fix: "...and every structure in it is referenced to a galaxy rather than to the Earth."

findings.field: straw_man.detail ("its principal critique in Nature Astronomy in 2022")
findings.problem: The entry dates Sawala et al. two ways. The sources list, the docstring and the steelman all say 2023; straw_man.detail says 2022. Both are defensible in isolation — the article was published online 19 December 2022 and carries the citation line Nature Astronomy volume 7, pages 481-491 (2023) — but a reader who notices the mismatch has no way to know which we mean, and curmudgeon.md lists edition and date confusion as one of the four recurring failures with six confirmed instances.
findings.fix: Make straw_man.detail read "its principal critique in Nature Astronomy in 2023 (online December 2022)", matching the sources list.

findings.field: sources (ROSAT entry; and the Jansen entry)
findings.problem: Two source labels claim slightly more than their URLs carry. The ROSAT label reads "scanning on great circles perpendicular to the ecliptic plane, which is why the deepest exposure and a run of cluster papers sit at the North Ecliptic Pole", but the cited Wikipedia page supports only the scanning geometry — it says the spacecraft performed "scanning observations on great circles perpendicular to the plane of the ecliptic" and carries nothing about exposure depth at the poles. The geometric inference is sound and the RASS North Ecliptic Pole deep survey is real, but the reader following the link will not find the second half. Separately, the Jansen source is labelled "Jansen et al." for a two-author paper (Jansen & Windhorst) and its title is trimmed to "field selection" where the paper is "...I: Field Selection of a JWST Community Field for Time-Domain Studies".
findings.fix: Split the ROSAT label so the URL only carries the scanning claim, and add a citation for the NEP deep exposure (the ROSAT NEP survey literature) alongside it. Change "Jansen et al." to "Jansen & Windhorst" and restore the subtitle.

findings.field: steelman.description, DEEPER paragraph ("with an RMS height of about 29 kpc (Pawlowski, Pflamm-Altenburg & Kroupa 2012)")
findings.problem: The 28.9 kpc figure is the RMS height of the Disc of Satellites — the satellites alone — and it originates with Kroupa et al. 2010; PPK12 reproduces and tabulates it under that attribution ("the DoS ... 156.4 -2.2 ... Kroupa et al. (2010)", and "the half-thickness or height of the DoS is 28.9 kpc"). The sentence attaches it instead to the composite structure of "satellites, young halo globular clusters and stellar streams", which has no single 29 kpc height — the same paper gives the young-halo globular-cluster plane an RMS height of 11.8 kpc. The docstring gets the provenance right ("Kroupa et al. 2010, as tabulated by Pawlowski et al. 2012 Table 1"); only the published sentence conflates.
findings.fix: "...share one highly inclined plane from 10 to 250 kpc out, with the satellite disc itself having an RMS height of about 29 kpc (Kroupa et al. 2010, tabulated in Pawlowski, Pflamm-Altenburg & Kroupa 2012)." Optionally add the 11.8 kpc globular-cluster plane height, which strengthens the steelman rather than weakening it.

findings.problem: The block says the book "attributes to the analysts a claim about the CMB rest frame removing the Pioneer effect, which reads as a paraphrase of a position not located in the two JPL review papers the chapter otherwise follows closely (Nieto & Turyshev, CQG 21:4005; Anderson et al., Phys. Rev. D 65:082004)." It IS located in Anderson et al. 2002. Sec. XI of gr-qc/0104064 reports Rosales and Sanchez-Gomez's proposal that "the Pioneer effect represents a new cosmological Foucault experiment", that "the Pioneers are mimicking the role that the rotating Earth plays in Foucault's experiment", and that "a coordinate transformation to the co-moving cosmological coordinate frame would entirely remove the Pioneer effect." The book's Claim #5 (printed p. 408) is a close and substantially faithful paraphrase of that paragraph. The absence claim is correctly scoped and factually false, and it accuses the source of inventing a position it in fact reported accurately.
findings.fix: Replace the last sentence of straw_man.detail with the accurate and sharper version: the book's Claim #5 tracks Anderson et al. 2002 Sec. XI (Rosales and Sanchez-Gomez) closely, but substitutes "Cosmic Microwave Background rest frame" for the paper's "co-moving cosmological coordinate frame" — two different frames, and the substitution is the book's, not the paper's. That is a real, small misrendering and it is checkable; the current sentence is not.

findings.field: refutation (section 5, 'The force the geocentric reading needs cannot exist')
findings.problem: The sentence "Anderson et al. noted in 2002 that the acceleration “is too large to have escaped detection in planetary orbits, particularly for Earth and Mars.”" puts quotation marks around wording that is not Anderson's. Anderson et al. 2002 reads: "The anomalous acceleration is too large to have gone undetected in planetary orbits, particularly for Earth and Mars." The phrase "escaped detection" is Sungenis & Bennett's, from numbered detail 2 at printed p. 401 of the Vol. II OCR: "Large, bound astronomical bodies show no signs of the anomaly, although the acceleration is too large to have escaped detection in planetary orbits, particularly for Earth and Mars." The reviewed book's paraphrase is being published as the reviewed paper's words, on a page whose subject is exactly that failure mode.
findings.fix: Quote Anderson as "too large to have gone undetected in planetary orbits, particularly for Earth and Mars". Then use the book's detail 2 in its own right as a second, stronger concession alongside detail 15 — the source states the planetary-orbit objection itself, in its own numbered list, which is a better find than the one currently claimed.

findings.problem: "The Pioneer anomaly really did point at the Earth — and that is how it was solved" is stronger than every source cited and stronger than the body, which quotes Turyshev et al. 2011 saying "although the direction of the acceleration remains imprecisely determined, we find no support in favor of a Sun-pointing direction over the Earth-pointing or along the spin-axis directions". Turyshev et al. 2012 puts it as "the direction of the anomalous acceleration cannot be determined unambiguously" while "the Doppler residuals improve if one considers a temporally varying acceleration in the direction of the Earth", and calls that merely "suggestive". The 2011 paper adds that "the spin and Earth-spacecraft axes are effectively degenerate". The second clause is also wrong historically: the case was closed by a finite-element thermal model cross-checked against an independent Doppler fit, not by the direction determination. The same overstatement recurs in the refutation ("The direction really did resolve towards the Earth") one clause before the quote that contradicts it, and in the steelman ("the best-fit direction really is Earth-pointing").
findings.fix: TLDR: "The Pioneer anomaly's direction was never pinned down — but the Doppler residuals improve if it points at the Earth, and that is a prediction of the answer, not a problem for it." Then keep the thermal sentence. In the refutation, replace "really did resolve towards the Earth" with the 2012 paper's own formulation (residuals improve for an Earth-directed, temporally varying acceleration; the spin and Earth-spacecraft axes are effectively degenerate), which concedes what the defender is owed without asserting what the papers decline to assert.

findings.field: refutation (section 3, 'The formula has since failed a prediction, in public')
findings.problem: The section loads weight on "four encounters consistent with zero from August 2005 onward, and a description that fits the first group and mispredicts the second", and the advocate.preemptive doubles down ("the load then rests ... on the four post-2007 nulls"). Only one of the four is a genuine misprediction. The entry itself quotes Anderson & Nieto's caveat that the relation models the anomaly "at least for flybys at an altitude of 2000 km or less"; Rosetta II's perigee altitude was 5,322 km and Rosetta III's 2,483 km, both outside that domain, so "where the relation expects a signal" is contestable on the entry's own quoted authority. MESSENGER (2,336 km) is predicted near-zero by the formula, which the entry says two sentences earlier — so counting it among encounters the description "mispredicts" contradicts the same paragraph. Juno (561 km) is the only clean out-of-sample failure, and the section already says so.
findings.fix: Rewrite the closing sentence to: three unexplained encounters 1990-2005; then MESSENGER, which the formula itself predicts near-zero; then Rosetta II and III, both above the 2,000 km altitude at which its authors scoped it; then Juno, at 561 km, inside the domain, predicted ~6 mm/s and measured 0 +/- 0.8. One clean failure, correctly identified, is a better argument than four nulls that a defender can dismantle in a sentence.

findings.field: refutation, chronology of the Juno prediction
findings.problem: "Iorio published the prediction beforehand" is false. Juno's Earth flyby was 9 October 2013; Iorio's paper is arXiv:1311.4218, submitted November 2013, and its own abstract reads "It predicts an anomaly of the order of 6 mm s^-1 for the recent flyby of Juno, occurred on 9 October 2013" — past tense. The prediction was published after the encounter and before the reconstruction (Thompson et al. 2014), which is still a real out-of-sample test but not a pre-registered one. The word "beforehand" is doing rhetorical work a defender will strip out.
findings.fix: "Iorio computed what the Anderson relation demanded — roughly 6 mm/s — and showed that nothing in classical or relativistic gravitation could produce it, before the flyby had been reconstructed. Thompson and colleagues at JPL then reconstructed it and found 0 +/- 0.8 mm/s."

findings.field: clusters.py E08 (renders next to the verdict chip, contradicting this entry)
findings.problem: The docstring reports this upward but the integrator must apply it, and it is the recurring failure the sweep called highest-leverage.
