The cluster note calls the flyby anomaly "an unreplicated 1990s Doppler-tracking puzzle ... a navigation problem, not a cosmological one", while the refutation says it is unexplained, cites Rosetta I in March 2005, and the advocate block warns in terms that "'a navigation problem' asserts a resolution nobody has published, and a defender who catches us doing that gets to discredit the section on the one point where we agree with him." The page would publish both. "Unreplicated" is also wrong on its face: six encounters were fitted, three with significant signals, across NASA and ESA. real_source cites only Pioneer papers though two of the three items are flyby items.
findings.fix: Anchor the edit on the cluster key, never on the originator= line. Note: "The Pioneer anomaly was resolved in 2012 — anisotropic thermal recoil. The flyby anomaly is real and unexplained: Galileo I, NEAR and Rosetta I gained 3.92, 13.46 and 1.82 mm/s, and every encounter since August 2005 has been consistent with zero. Its one empirical description is proportional to the Earth's sidereal rotation rate." real_source: add "Anderson et al. 2008, PRL 100:091102".

findings.field: refutation (section 4, 'Why the anomalies happen at Earth')
findings.problem: "the Deep Space Network provides that only for encounters with our own planet" is false as written, and is contradicted two paragraphs later by the entry's own Acedo citation — Acedo, Piqueras and Morano's Jupiter claim is built from exactly this kind of two-way coherent Doppler through Juno's perijove. The DSN also tracked Cassini coherently through Saturn periapses. The true point is fractional precision and the quality of the local gravity-field and ephemeris models, not availability.
findings.fix: "Detecting a millimetre-per-second residual requires two-way coherent Doppler through closest approach against a gravity field, atmosphere and ephemeris known to parts in 10^9 — a combination only the Earth currently offers. Perijove and periapse tracking exists, at far coarser fractional precision." That also makes the Acedo paragraph land as reinforcement rather than as a contradiction.

findings.problem: "It is not evidence of anything cosmological, and no one in the field has proposed that it is" is an unscoped universal negative about an entire literature — the project's dominant confirmed failure mode, in a phrasing the ratcheting regex does not catch ("proposed" is not in its verb list, so the test is green and the rule is broken). It also has a live counterexample: Adler, "Can the flyby anomaly be attributed to earth-bound dark matter?", Phys. Rev. D 79:023505 (2009), arXiv:0805.2895, proposes a dark-matter halo bound to the Earth.
findings.fix: "It is not evidence of anything cosmological. The exotic proposals that have been published — Adler's earth-bound dark matter (Phys. Rev. D 79:023505, 2009) among them — put something unusual around the Earth; none of them puts the Earth at the centre of anything, and no paper located in this search argues that it does."

findings.field: tldr and refutation (section 1, the thermal budget)
findings.problem: The 63 W figure and the 2,578 W figure belong to different epochs. Q_rtg = 2578.179 W is Turyshev et al. 2012's value at t0 = 1 July 1972, decaying as 2^(-(t-t0)/87.74); the 8.74e-10 m/s^2 fit comes from Doppler data taken over 20-78 AU, i.e. roughly 1983-1998, by which time the RTG thermal output is about 2,100 W. The ratio is therefore about 3%, not 2.4%. The body at least labels the epoch; the TLDR pairs "63 watts" with "2,578 watts of plutonium heat" as if simultaneous, and the paragraph brands the figure as recomputed here, which invites the check.
findings.fix: State it as "about 63 W of net one-sided radiation — roughly 3% of the RTG heat still available over the fit interval, which was about 2,100 W by the late 1990s from a launch value of 2,578 W". Same argument, and it survives the recomputation a defender will do.

findings.field: passage.gloss and compression.note, provenance of the Pioneer/flyby pairing
findings.problem: The compression note says item 191 "reproduces the book's own pairing of the two", and the gloss calls the book "the earliest text located that carries both halves of this cluster, in the order and pairing the list uses". The two halves sit ~380 pages apart in different chapters, and the only place they appear together is ch. 7, n. 58 — where the pairing is Lammerzahl, Preuss and Dittus's, being summarised. The OCR is explicit: "In addition to the Pioneer anomalies, the Lammerzahl team remark on the 'flyby' anomalies". On a project whose product is the chain, attributing an inherited pairing to the book misplaces a link.
findings.fix: "The two halves are paired in one place in the reachable text — ch. 7, n. 58 — and the pairing there is Lammerzahl, Preuss and Dittus's, which the footnote is summarising. The book carries the pairing; it did not make it." This also strengthens the entry's existing point that nothing in this cluster originates with the movement.

findings.field: passage.gloss, "Sungenis and Bennett reproduce that mapping unchanged"
findings.problem: True of the pp. 406-407 passage the gloss is describing — I checked it against gr-qc/0308017 and the four directions and four inferences are carried over almost verbatim — but the same chapter renders the list a second time, at numbered detail 7, printed p. 402, with FIVE origins: "(a) new dynamical physics originating from the sun; (b) a time signal anomaly; (c) a drag or inertial effect; (d) a property of the ether flow in the outer solar system; (e) an on-board systematic defect." A defender of the book will produce detail 7 against the bolded "unchanged". The insertion is also the best single piece of evidence for the entry's own claim that the book's preferred cause is a variable ether, so leaving it out costs twice.
findings.fix: Add one clause: the book prints the JPL list twice — unchanged at pp. 406-407, and at detail 7 (p. 402) with an ether option inserted as a fifth origin that is not in Nieto and Turyshev. Then the ether point is documented rather than asserted.

findings.field: refutation (section 3) and sources[] flyby table label
findings.problem: Rosetta III's "-0.004 +/- 0.044 mm/s" is the speed increment at perigee, not the increment at infinity; the Δv-infinity entry for Rosetta III is ~0. The paragraph is about the Anderson relation, which is written in Δv-infinity, so two frames are being mixed. Separately, Galileo II (8 Dec 1992, -4.60 +/- 1.00 mm/s at infinity) is absent from both the narrative list and the source label's table, though it is one of the six encounters Anderson et al. 2008 fitted and it is a 4.6-sigma negative result inside the era the entry describes as "three clearly unexplained encounters".
findings.fix: Use ~0 for Rosetta III at infinity, or say explicitly that the -0.004 +/- 0.044 figure is the perigee increment. Add Galileo II with the standard caveat — 303 km perigee, confounded by atmospheric drag — which is a stronger position than omitting it.

findings.field: passage.locator and sources[] (the Vol. II scan label)
findings.problem: Locator precision, checked against the OCR page markers. The numbered details run across two pages: items 1-7 on printed p. 401, items 8-15 on p. 402 — so detail 15, which the entry leans on three times, is on p. 402, while the label says "the numbered details at p. 401". "Claims and Responses" begins on p. 407 (Claim #1 sits directly under the four-direction passage); only the Response to Claim #1 onward is on p. 408. The entry's "at printed p. 408" for the response is right; "the section, at printed p. 408" is not.
findings.fix: "numbered details at pp. 401-402 (detail 6 at p. 401, detail 15 at p. 402); the four directions at pp. 406-407; 'Claims and Responses' at pp. 407-408, the Response to Claim #1 at p. 408."

findings.problem: "Anderson et al. describe the attitude manoeuvres as keeping the Earth inside about one degree of the dish's axis" loosens the source by a factor of two. Anderson et al. 2002: "Regular changes of the attitude of the spacecraft are performed throughout the mission to keep the Earth within the narrow beam of about one degree full width of the spacecraft-fixed parabolic antenna." One degree full width is half a degree from the axis. The 3.6-degree half-power downlink cone quoted alongside it is correct and verbatim.
findings.fix: "...keeping the Earth inside a beam about one degree wide" — which is also the stronger number for the argument being made.

findings.field: sources[] — Nature Physics label, and refutation quotation
findings.problem: The quotation "Once again, the mundane possibilities have won out against exotic, new-physics explanations" could not be verified from the reachable portion of nphys2428. Title, volume, page and year all check out ("...and farewell to the Pioneer anomaly", Nature Physics 8:635, 2012), and the accessible opening paragraph contains "there were several mundane possibilities to explore" in a different sentence, which raises the possibility of a conflation. Unreachable is not wrong, but this is the only quotation in the entry I could not put eyes on.
findings.fix: Either verify against the full editorial and leave it, or scope it: attribute the farewell framing to the editorial without the verbatim sentence. Everything else in the paragraph carries the weight already.

findings.problem: The TLDR's punchline is "the astronomer behind the 2025 headlines says 'our galaxy', not 'the Earth'", and compression.note lists "The referent moves" as one of three things the list changed in transit. Banik's quoted words are indeed "our galaxy" — but the single source we cite for that quote is the University of Portsmouth / RAS National Astronomy Meeting release, whose headline reads "Is Earth inside a huge void? 'Sound of the Big Bang' hints at possible solution to Hubble tension" and whose body says verbatim: "For the idea to stand up, Earth and our solar system would need to be near the centre of a void about a billion light-years in radius and with a density about 20 per cent below the average for the universe as a whole." The Earth-referent is already there, in the professional communication of the result, before any proof list touched it — and it is visible in the URL slug sitting in our own `sources` array (is-earth-inside-a-huge-void-...). A defender who clicks the one link we give for this argument lands on a page that appears to refute our headline sentence in its title.
findings.fix: Do not drop the point — extend it, because the extension is the project's own thesis. Keep "Banik says 'our galaxy'" but state where the substitution actually happens: the referent moves in the press release, not on the list, and the list inherited it. Suggested TLDR clause: "...the astronomer behind the 2025 headlines says 'our galaxy'; his own university's press release had already turned that into 'Earth and our solar system', and the list inherited the swap rather than inventing it." In compression.note, rename the second drift from "The referent moves" to something like "The referent had already moved", and cite the release's own sentence — a drift that begins in science communication and is then hardened by a proof list is a stronger finding for this project than one the list manufactured alone, and it removes the entry's most clickable vulnerability.

findings.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim and refutation §7 (the 15 Mpc centring tolerance)
findings.problem: The entry's decisive quantitative move — the docstring calls it "THE DECISIVE NUMBER" — is Alnes & Amarzguioui's ~15 Mpc centring bound. The quote is verbatim and correctly attributed. But their §V states the scale of the model it was computed for: "When compared to the size of the underdensity, which according to Fig. 2 is around 1500 Mpc...". That is a dark-energy-replacing LTB bubble roughly five times the extent of the ~300 Mpc KBC void the section is discussing, and §7 imports the number straight across ("out to something like 300 Mpc ... How near is set by the microwave dipole: Alnes & Amarzguioui found for their model that the observer must lie within about 15 Mpc"). The scoping phrase "for their model" is present, but the conclusion drawn from it is not scoped: "The centring constraint is a ball roughly 3.6e16 Earth diameters wide", "a hypothesis whose finest available 'here' is a ball 49 million light-years wide". Worse, advocate.best_defense raises exactly this attack ("Your fifteen-megaparsec figure comes from one 2006 paper about one void profile — hardly a law of nature") and advocate.preemptive answers it by restating the same number ("a hypothesis with a 49-million-light-year resolution cannot express the proposition 'the Earth rather than the Sun'"), which is circular. No centring constraint specific to the KBC/Banik void is cited anywhere in the entry.
findings.fix: Add the insensitivity argument, which is the real answer and costs one sentence: the conclusion does not depend on the number. Something like: "That bound is computed for Alnes & Amarzguioui's own model, a ~1500 Mpc underdensity built to replace dark energy, and no equivalent bound has been published for the shallower ~300 Mpc void at issue here. It does not matter which way that number moves. The Earth-Sun distance is 5e-12 Mpc; the tolerance would have to tighten by more than fifteen orders of magnitude before the hypothesis could express the sentence 'the Earth rather than the Sun'." Then rewrite the preemptive to point at the insensitivity rather than at the 49-million-light-year figure.

findings.field: scripts/clusters.py, cluster E09 `note` (renders as the basis line under the verdict chip, scripts/render.py line 180)
findings.problem: The cluster note reads: "The local-void reading was tested directly on 1295 supernovae and excluded at 4-5σ." Kenworthy, Scolnic & Riess exclude, at 4-5σ, sharp-edged LTB underdensities with |delta| > 20% (5σ bound delta < 27% on scales above 69 h^-1 Mpc) — verified against their abstract. They do not exclude "the local-void reading", which is being argued in MNRAS as of 2025 by Banik & Kalaitzidis and which this treatment's §5 concedes at full strength. The basis line therefore states flatly the one thing §5, §6 and the TLDR go out of their way not to say, and it renders in the summary line next to the verdict chip, where skim readers who never expand the entry will meet it. The treatment's docstring note 3 diagnoses this correctly and, correctly per the house rule, did not edit clusters.py or comment on our record in the published prose — so this survives as an integrator action, and it is the E01/E03 "reported, NOT ACTUALLY APPLIED" pattern recurring.
findings.fix: Integrator: edit scripts/clusters.py anchored on the cluster key "E09", never on a positional line. Replace the note with something the body supports, e.g.: "Two rival explanations of one number, counted as two proofs. Kenworthy et al. 2019 exclude sharp-edged voids deeper than 20% at 4-5σ on 1295 supernovae; a shallower local void is still argued in MNRAS. Either way the region is tens to hundreds of megaparsecs across and does not single out the Earth." Also record the change in review/corrections.json — the old line is a published overstatement, not merely a stale one.

findings.field: refutation §2 and tldr ("the two items cancel" / "each one kills the other")
findings.problem: §2 asserts the two items are "two mutually exclusive candidate explanations" and that "each one kills the other"; the docstring calls them "two mutually exclusive escapes" and the TLDR says "the two items cancel". They are rival explanations, not mutually exclusive ones. Nothing prevents a partial calibration systematic and a partial local underdensity both contributing, and combinations of that kind are discussed in the literature the entry is otherwise scrupulous about. The conditional in §2 ("If the first is true, the 73 is an artefact, there is no discrepancy, and nothing remains") silently assumes each hypothesis explains the whole 5.6 km/s/Mpc gap — but Freedman's own best TRGB value, 70.39, still sits about 2σ above Planck's 67.4, so even on the observation-bias reading a residual is left. A well-informed defender gets a free hit here ("we offered two candidate explanations; you invented the claim that we assert both jointly"), and advocate.best_defense does not raise it, so nothing in the entry absorbs it.
findings.fix: Downgrade the modal claim and keep the real point, which survives intact: they are rival explanations that the list scores as two independent witnesses, and neither reaches the conclusion. Replace "mutually exclusive" with "rival", replace "each one kills the other" with "each subtracts from the other", and add the quantitative version: "they compete for the same 5.6 km/s/Mpc, so to the extent the ladder carries a systematic there is less gap left for a void to fill — and Freedman's own best value still sits about 2σ from Planck, so neither hypothesis has yet claimed the whole of it." Mirror the change in the TLDR's "the two items cancel".

findings.field: tldr and refutation §11 (the closing verdict paragraph)
findings.problem: Both misdescribe the size of the thing the void models are about. The TLDR says "the 'special location' those models describe is a region tens of megaparsecs across centred on the Local Group", and the verdict paragraph says the location reading concerns "the mean density of a region 49 million light-years across, at best, around the Local Group". The models describe an underdensity extending to about 300 Mpc — Banik & Kalaitzidis's abstract opens "a local void approximately 20 per cent underdense extending to 300 Mpc", and the RAS release says about a billion light-years in radius. The tens-of-megaparsecs figure is the centring tolerance for the observer, not the region whose mean density is at issue; §7 keeps the two straight and the TLDR and the closing line do not. This is the recurring pattern where the TLDR is written from memory of the argument: it takes the number that does the rhetorical work and attaches it to the wrong noun, and a defender's first move is "they do not even know how big the void is".
findings.fix: Separate the two scales in both places. TLDR: "...the models describe an underdensity hundreds of megaparsecs across around the Local Group, inside which the observer's position is pinned only to a few tens of megaparsecs — which cannot tell the Earth apart from Andromeda, let alone from the Sun." Closing paragraph: "...on the location reading it is the mean density of a region some 300 Mpc across, with our position inside it pinned no more finely than a few tens of megaparsecs."

findings.problem: The field closes: "There is also an implied suppression the record does not support: every result on both sides of this cluster is in the open refereed literature...". Items 98 and 325 are three-word noun phrases — "Hubble tension observation bias." and "Hubble tension location bias." — and neither carries or implies a suppression claim. Attributing an implication to the item in order to answer it is precisely the move the hedge rule exists to forbid, done in the one field whose job is to catch that move being done to us; the irony is available to any defender who quotes the two items back at us. (The rest of the field is excellent and well sourced.)
findings.fix: Delete the "implied suppression" clause, or re-anchor it to something the record actually shows — if a neighbouring item in the same run carries a concealment framing, quote that item by number instead of inferring the implication from a noun phrase. The positive half of the sentence is worth keeping on its own: that every result on both sides is in the open literature and that the void story was the RAS's own press item is a fact about the cluster, not a rebuttal of an imputed charge.

findings.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, refutation §7, compression.note (radius stated as diameter)
findings.problem: Alnes & Amarzguioui's 15 Mpc is a radius — "located within a radius of ~15 Mpc from the center", quoted correctly in our own text, and their eq. (30) is d_obs <~ 15 Mpc. The entry then converts it as though it were a diameter in four places: "Fifteen megaparsecs is about 49 million light-years" followed by "a ball 49 million light-years wide"; "The centring constraint is a ball roughly 3.6 x 10^16 Earth diameters wide"; "a region 49 million light-years across"; and in compression.note "a resolution roughly 3.6 x 10^16 times finer". The ball is ~30 Mpc, about 98 million light-years across, and about 7.3 x 10^16 Earth diameters wide. Docstring note 6 shows the arithmetic and makes the slip visible: it divides the radius by the Earth's diameter. The error runs in the conservative direction and changes nothing, but it is checkable in one line by anyone hostile.
findings.fix: Either say radius throughout ("a ball of radius 49 million light-years", "a radius roughly 3.6 x 10^16 Earth diameters") or double the diameters (98 million light-years, 7.3 x 10^16). Fix the docstring arithmetic line at the same time so the next writer does not inherit it.

findings.field: refutation §3 ("Not one of them says anything about the Earth's shape, motion or position")
findings.problem: An unscoped universal negative over an entire live literature: "every proposition in that dispute is about the photometry of variable stars in ten to forty other galaxies. Not one of them says anything about the Earth's shape, motion or position." This is the banned construction wearing different clothes — the house rule is to scope an absence to the specific text searched, and the ratcheting test in tests/test_provenance.py (currently green at 4/4) does not scan the refutation body, which is exactly how the batch-8 sweep found the rule failing while its test stayed green. It is also pedantically false in a way a defender can exploit: barycentric corrections for the Earth's own orbital motion are applied throughout precision distance-ladder work.
findings.fix: Scope it to what was read: "Across the papers cited in this section — Riess et al. 2022 and 2024, Freedman et al. 2024, Kenworthy et al. 2019 — the subject matter is the photometry and calibration of variable stars in other galaxies; the Earth enters only as the platform the observations are corrected for."

findings.problem: "To make the comb appear you must first place the observer on a body moving at all three of those speeds and take them out" is false for the periodicity the entry leads with, and it contradicts the sentence two lines above it. Napier & Guthrie's 37.5 km/s comb is galactocentric: two subtractions. Humphreys' own text (p. 96) says the galactocentric redshift compensates "for the Earth's motion around the Sun and the Sun's motion around our galaxy's centre"; the 556 km/s CMB step is a further transformation used in Tifft's CBR-rest-frame papers, which is what the entry's own preceding sentence ("Tifft's own later refinement went further in the same direction") already says. Bajan et al. say "galactocentric radial velocities OR using CMB reference frame" — either two or three, not all three. The TLDR gets this right ("galactocentric or microwave-background"); the body overstates it. Worse, this exact point is the source's own printed rebuttal, unanswered here: Bennett, Vol. II ch. 10, printed p. 298 of the same three-volume scan the entry quotes — "subtraction or correction is only done for the first two motions - the orbit around the sun and the solar motion around the galaxy center, the galactocentric frame of reference! The Milky Way motion and the motion towards Leo were unknown at the time and were not taken into account, yet they represent the largest component of the Earth's motion - about 600 km/s! ... Unless, of course, the motions of the Earth are fictitious!" Neither the refutation nor advocate.best_defense engages it, so the strongest form of the source's answer to our load-bearing section goes unmet.
findings.fix: Replace "all three of those speeds" with "the first two of those speeds", and add a short paragraph to section II answering Bennett: the answer is in the book's own footnote on printed p. 417, which lists Tifft's CBR-rest-frame papers (Astrophysics and Space Science 239:35, 1996; J. Astrophys. Astr. 18:415, 1997), i.e. the periodicity is also reported after the full ~600 km/s is removed. So the geocentric reading has to call the corrections fictitious in one frame while spending a result that only exists in another. Add the Vol. II p. 298 passage to advocate.best_defense so the page is seen to have met it.

findings.field: clusters.py E12 (note and real_source) - renders as the published basis line
findings.problem: The cluster note reads "Quantization disappeared as sample sizes grew; the effect was an artefact of small, sparse redshift samples" and real_source reads "Tifft 1976; refuted by 2dF/SDSS surveys". build.py:156 renders that note as the argument's basis line beside the verdict chip, where it is read by people who never expand the entry - and section IV of this treatment exists specifically to refuse both sentences ("Two sigma is not nothing and this page will not call it nothing"; "the honest statement is that the effect shrank drastically when the selection was removed, not that it vanished"; and on 2dF, "That is the Burbidge-Karlsson claim, not Tifft's 37.5 km/s comb, and using it as though it settled this cluster is sloppy"). The docstring's report-up list (note 1) names originator, originator_work, year and real_source but not note, so the contradicting line would not have been fixed. This is recurring failure #5 in review/curmudgeon.md for at least the fifth time. Minor detail in the same place: note 1's cross-reference "(see note 4)" points at the Humphreys-criterion note; the real_source/2dF discussion is note 5.
findings.fix: Report up the note as well, anchored on the cluster key "E12" and never on the originator= line. Proposed replacement basis: "The periodicity survives only in frames defined by the Earth's motion, and the shell reading fails its own author's blurring criterion by a factor of eight; large-sample tests reduce it to ~2 sigma rather than eliminating it." Proposed real_source: "Tifft 1972-1984; Napier & Guthrie 1997 (galactocentric); Humphreys TJ 16(2), 2002." Fix "(see note 4)" to "(see note 5)".

findings.field: passage.gloss (para 3) and compression.note ("Two: a scope is widened...")
findings.problem: The Sungenis-to-Humphreys link is asserted rather than shown, and the two specifics offered as evidence do not survive checking. In the OCR text this entry uses (Internet Archive item galileo-was-wrong-the-church-was-right-sungenis-vol-1-3-complete, 5,499,250 bytes), the section at printed pp. 417-420 argues from Tifft, a Sky & Telescope item, Matthews in Science and Koo & Kron; none of Humphreys' geometry, arithmetic or one-in-a-trillion figure is located anywhere in that text, and no figure caption crediting Humphreys is located in it either - so "once reproduces a figure from" is unsupported by the entry's own stated provenance route (docstring note 7). "Cites twice by title" is also wrong: the title is located at printed pp. 284, 398, 432 and 580, in the bibliography at p. 631, and in a web-link list at p. 694. So the section does not compress Humphreys' derivation; it argues in parallel with it. This matters because compression.note's second published finding ("a scope is widened by about nine orders of magnitude") is built on the section being downstream of Humphreys.
findings.fix: Keep the finding, drop the chain claim. The part that verifies, and it is enough, is the p. 398 footnote: the book cites Humphreys' TJ paper by title and records that he holds the galaxy, not the Earth, to be the centre, and that "Both Humphreys and Gentry posit that the Earth has diurnal and translational motion" - then heads its own section "Centered Around the Earth" anyway. Rewrite as "the same argument in its strongest published form belongs to someone who rejects the conclusion - and the book cites him by title at pp. 398 and 432 and names him as a galactocentric rival", delete "twice" and delete the figure claim (or supply a page).

findings.problem: "...which is why Tifft, who found the pattern, read it as a property of redshift rather than as a map" states a causal claim about a named astronomer's reasoning that nothing in the entry sources. The only Tifft text the entry carries is the "imprinted ... microscopic quantum physics" sentence, quoted at second hand from Galileo Was Wrong (printed p. 418), which gives his conclusion and not his reason. straw_man.detail goes further - "Tifft gave that answer; the book prints it, and reads it as evasion" - but what the book prints is the conclusion, not the peculiar-velocity reasoning. Neither Tifft 1976 nor Tifft & Cocke 1984 was read for this entry (the sources block bundles both under one label whose URL points at the 1976 abstract). This is the sweep's #6 pattern: the TLDR carries a specific the cited source does not contain.
findings.fix: Either cite Tifft where he argues it - Tifft, "Discrete states of redshift and galaxy dynamics I: internal motions in single galaxies", ApJ 206:38 (1976), which is about internal dynamics and is the natural locator - or mark it as our inference: "...which is why the pattern cannot be a pattern in distance at all, and why its discoverer placed it in the redshift instead." In straw_man, replace "Tifft gave that answer; the book prints it" with "the book prints his conclusion and reads it as evasion."

findings.problem: "The second is the word Earth, which is not in the astronomy being cited" is an unscoped absence claim over a body of papers this entry did not search. Napier & Guthrie were read at abstract and conclusion level, Bajan et al. as a review, and Tifft only through Galileo Was Wrong's quotations. As literally written it is also loose: the galactocentric correction is defined by removing the Earth's orbital motion, so "Earth" is in the astronomy. The repo's lint would not catch this - it is a paraphrase around _ABSENCE, which is the documented failure mode ("writers have learned the regex, not the rule").
findings.fix: Rescope to the text actually read: "The second is the word Earth. What is not in the papers this entry reads - Napier and Guthrie's 1997 status report and Bajan and colleagues' review - is any claim that the groups are centred on the Earth; in both, the frame is galactocentric and the Earth's motion is what gets removed."

findings.field: compression.note ("Two: a scope is widened by about nine orders of magnitude")
findings.problem: The number does not match the comparison it is attached to. The note explains itself as the width of a galaxy arriving on a proof list as a statement about a planet: 100,000 light years against the Earth's diameter is about fourteen orders of magnitude, not nine. About nine is what you get comparing the galaxy's diameter to the Earth's orbit (~2 AU), a comparison the note never states. A defender who checks the arithmetic in a headline finding will use the mismatch.
findings.fix: Drop the figure and let the concrete comparison carry it: "Two: a bound whose stated resolution is the diameter of the Galaxy arrives on a proof list as a statement about a planet." Or state the comparison being made explicitly.

findings.problem: "the peaks are sharp - some of them, Humphreys notes, only a few km/s wide" attributes to Humphreys a statement about peak width he does not make. His text quotes Tifft and Cocke's phrase "sharp periodicities at exact submultiples (1/3 and 1/2) of 72.45 km/s" and lists finer observed intervals at 2.6, 9.15 and 18.3 km/s. Those are spacings, not widths. The inference is fair; the attribution is not.
findings.fix: "the intervals are fine - Humphreys lists observed periodicities as small as 2.6 km/s - and galaxies move at hundreds of km/s, so a pattern that survives at all cannot be a pattern in distance."

findings.field: passage.gloss (para 2) and compression.note ("One: an interpretation is reversed")
findings.problem: Both say the Tifft "imprinted" quotation is printed "two pages later". Per the Internet Archive item's own leaf-to-page metadata, the section heading and the quoted sentence are on printed p. 417 (leaf 430) and the Tifft block quotation is on p. 418 (leaf 431) - one page later. The same metadata confirms the passage.locator's "printed p. 417" is correct, so only the interval is wrong.
findings.fix: Change both instances of "two pages later" to "on the next page".

findings.problem: Citation hygiene, three small things. (a) Section I presents "very firm evidence that the redshifts of galaxies are quantized with a primary interval near 72 km s-1" as what Tifft "wrote in ApJ 287:492 (1984)", but the entry's stated provenance route is the Sungenis OCR footnote at p. 417 (the sentence is also quoted in Humphreys p. 96); the ApJ paper was not read. Two independent secondaries agree, so the attribution is probably right, but the page does not say it is quoted at second hand. (b) The Tifft sources entry bundles the 1976 and 1984 papers under one label whose URL resolves only to the 1976 abstract. (c) The Bajan label cites Phys. Part. Nucl. Lett. 4(1):5-11 (2007), which is correct for the Springer English edition (ADS 2007PPNL....4....5B), but the linked JINR PDF is paginated 16-24, and the paper states "the probability that they are coming from nonrandom distribution is 95%" where our text says "2 sigma" throughout without noting the conversion.
findings.fix: (a) Add "as quoted in Galileo Was Wrong p. 417 and in Humphreys p. 96; the 1984 paper was not read for this entry" to the Tifft source label. (b) Split the 1976 and 1984 entries or point the URL at the 1984 record. (c) Add "(JINR PDF paginated 16-24)" to the Bajan label, and in section IV write "at 95 per cent confidence, about two sigma" once.

findings.field: refutation (section "Fourth, the measurement, with the numbers")
findings.problem: Two numbers are attributed to Zhang & Stebbins, PRL 107:041301, but they exist only in the superseded arXiv v2, not in the published version the entry cites. We write "(SPT gives < 13 µK²)" and "miss the supernovae by Δχ² > 195". The published paper (arXiv v3, the one served at the abs URL in our own sources list) reads: "The South Pole telescope (SPT) collaboration [18] found ΔT² < 6.5µK² (95% upper limit) and the Atacama cosmology telescope (ACT) collaboration [19] found ΔT² < 8µK²", and "Hubble bubble models consistent with the SPT result have Δχ² > 209 (χ² > 814)". Version v2 does say 13 µK² and Δχ² > 195, so the source of the error is identifiable. The error also inverts the ranking of the two experiments: our parenthetical presents SPT as the looser bound, whereas in the published paper SPT is the tighter one and is the limit the headline "two orders of magnitude" comparison is made against. A defender who opens the cited paper finds this in the first column.
findings.fix: Replace "(SPT gives < 13 µK²)" with "(SPT, the tighter of the two, gives < 6.5 µK²)" and "Δχ² > 195" with "Δχ² > 209". Add "published version, arXiv v3" to the Zhang & Stebbins source label so the next writer does not re-import v2 figures, and correct the same two numbers in the module docstring's note 5.

findings.problem: The closing sentence claims the measurement "excludes by two orders of magnitude the only version of a non-Copernican universe anybody has built." That is an unscoped universal about an entire literature, of exactly the class the house rule bans, in a phrasing the ratchet regex does not match. It is also false on the evidence of the very page of Ellis arXiv:1103.2335 we rely on for the "typical observationally viable model": p. 15 says "Actually you don't need a void to explain the observations; more general models can do the job", and the same section reports Bolejko and Sussman arguing the improbability problem is eased with "a Szekeres rather than LTB solution". Section six carries the same overclaim in miniature ("What is on offer is a Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi void"). A defender only has to quote our own cited source back at us.
findings.fix: Rewrite the clause as scoped to what was tested: "...and excludes by two orders of magnitude the spherically symmetric LTB void models that were built to replace dark energy — the class the kSZ test was aimed at." In section six change "What is on offer is a Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi void" to "What has actually been built and fitted is a Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi void", and add Ellis's own caveat that more general models can do the job.

findings.problem: The refutation states the kSZ result as an unqualified exclusion and never publishes the survival window the cited paper states in the same paragraph as the numbers we do quote: "only models with Ω₀ → 1 or z_edge → 0 (z_edge < ~0.2, corresponding to void radius < 0.6 h⁻¹ Gpc) survive this test". The entry's own research note 5 records this qualification, so it was seen and then left out of the published prose. The omission has a visible consequence: section six's exemplar — Ellis's "typical observationally viable model", an underdense region of 160-250 h⁻¹ Mpc — sits well inside the surviving window, so the page excludes a class in section four and then illustrates the prize with a member of the class that survives, without telling the reader the two are different.
findings.fix: Add one sentence at the end of section four: "The paper is explicit about where the test stops: voids small enough that the underdensity ends below z ≈ 0.2 — radius under about 0.6 h⁻¹ Gpc — survive the kSZ bound, and are excluded instead by failing the supernovae, which is why the two tests are quoted together." Then in section six, mark Ellis's specimen as a member of that smaller class.

findings.field: clusters.py R12 `note` — renders as the summary line of the Refutation section on docs/index.html
findings.problem: The rendered one-line summary of our refutation reads "It is not merely assumed — it is tested. The kSZ power spectrum rules out Gpc-scale off-centre void models." The entry's own docstring note 7 judges this line unsupported by the paper and proposes a replacement, and records it as "Reported in record_problems; clusters.py NOT touched" — but there is no record_problems file in the repository, clusters.py is unchanged, and the line is live in docs/index.html directly under the REFUTED chip. "Off-centre" is also the wrong descriptor: the models at issue put us near the centre, and the off-centre observers are the distant ones whose motion sources the kSZ signal. This is the E01/E03 "recorded, not actually applied" pattern for at least the fifth time, in the most prominent position the cluster record reaches.
findings.fix: Edit clusters.py anchored on the "R12" key (never on the originator= line) so the note reads: "It is not merely assumed — it is tested. The kSZ power spectrum rules out the LTB void models deep enough to mimic dark energy." Rebuild and re-run tests/run.sh.

findings.problem: The cluster record credits the argument to "The Principle (film)", 2014, and row 354 of the published dataset carries that pair. The entry's own gloss argues the opposite and is right: the argument is the book's, the same paragraph is in the CD edition of Volume I (ISBN 0-9779640-0-0) at p. 145, and the passage cites WRK-SUNGENIS-2006. The byline "Robert Sungenis & Robert Bennett" belongs to the book; the film was produced by DeLano and Sungenis, as works.py itself records at WRK-PRINCIPLE-2014 and as ARG-E11 records. So the published provenance row pairs the book's authors with the film's title. On a project whose product is provenance this is the worst available place for it. It does not currently render on the argument card (render.py's meta line prints only the originator), which is why this is moderate rather than major.
findings.fix: Anchored on the "R12" key, set originator_work="Galileo Was Wrong: The Church Was Right, Vol. I" and year="2006", leaving the byline unchanged. Confirm post1950_cited_clusters still has ten members (2006 ≥ 1950, so it does) and rebuild.

findings.problem: The published quote opens "This clearly shows that the Copernican Principle..." and nothing in the locator or gloss says what "This" refers to. In the scan the referent is the two sentences immediately before, on the same page: Richard Wolfson's Teaching Company lecture 5, in which he grants that "a perfectly viable solution to the Michelson-Morley experiment is that the Earth is motionless" and then rules it out by appealing to the "Copernican Principle that the earth isn't special", adding that "it suffices to rule it out on this philosophical ground". That is the book's evidence for the charge we are answering, and it is the strongest thing at that location — our own advocate block ranks it as the defender's fifth move and the preemptive concedes it outright. Publishing the conclusion while suppressing the instance is the truncation this project exists to document, and it leaves the concession buried in the advocate block where a skimming reader never meets it.
findings.fix:
Add to the gloss, before "Read what is being claimed": "

What ‘this’ is. The sentence concludes an argument about one named lecture. On the same page the book quotes Richard Wolfson granting that a motionless Earth is a viable reading of Michelson–Morley and then setting it aside because ‘it suffices to rule it out on this philosophical ground’. The instance is fair and is conceded here: he had better arguments available and used a worse one, and the better ones are at ARG-A02 and ARG-A05. What does not follow is the generalisation the next sentence makes.

" Add A02 and A05 to `related`, since the preemptive already points at them.

findings.field: refutation (sections "Third"/pattern paragraph and "Fourth" lead-ins) — printed page numbers
findings.problem: Two printed-page citations are off by one against the scan the entry names. We write that Gale is "quoted at printed p. 309": the lead-in "One author put it this way:" ends p. 309 but the Gale block quote itself, including "until 1948 by Hermann Bondi of the University of Cambridge", is on p. 310. We write "At printed p. 320 it quotes Robert Caldwell": the Caldwell sentence is on p. 321. Both are wrong under the same page convention by which the entry's other three cites are right — the passage locator's p. 92, the a-priori line at p. 309 and the steelman's Ellis quote at p. 310 all check out, so this is an internal inconsistency in our own numbering rather than a disputed convention. Calibrated against three table-of-contents entries (chapter 2 at p. 125, "Is There a Copernican Conspiracy?" at p. 109, "Copernicus: More Epicycles than Ptolemy" at p. 56).
findings.fix: In section three change "quoted at printed p. 309" to "quoted at printed p. 310", and in the Caldwell paragraph change "At printed p. 320" to "At printed p. 321".

findings.problem: We write that Ellis is said to withhold the Earth as a rest frame "for reasons he does not reveal", "in a passage where the reason he gives is quoted two paragraphs earlier". In the scan (printed p. 311) the reason is in the block quote immediately preceding the accusation — the sentence directly before it: "The Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation determines the preferred rest frame (and associated time coordinate) to high accuracy." "Two paragraphs earlier" understates our own point and invites a needless correction.
findings.fix: Replace "quoted two paragraphs earlier" with "quoted in the block immediately above it".

findings.problem: We give the line as "I can construct you a spherically symmetrical universe with Earth at its center". The route we declare for this quotation is the book, since the magazine was paywalled, and the book prints it with an editorial insertion: "I can construct [for] you a spherically symmetrical universe with Earth at its center". Dropping a bracket while stating that the wording is reported at one remove is a small hole in a section whose whole value is that we quoted the opposition exactly.
findings.fix: Restore the bracket: "I can construct [for] you a spherically symmetrical universe with Earth at its center".

findings.problem: We say the centring tolerance "works out at tens of megaparsecs — the arithmetic is done at ARG-E09". E09's arithmetic gives ~15 Mpc (Alnes & Amarzguioui, the observer "has to be located within a radius of ~15 Mpc from the center"), which is not tens of megaparsecs. R12's own derivation — 10% of a 160-250 h⁻¹ Mpc region — does give 23-36 Mpc, so the two pages reach different numbers for the same quantity and the cross-link implies they are the same calculation. Harmless for the conclusion, since both are tens of millions of light-years, but it is the kind of cross-page inconsistency a critic collects.
findings.fix: Change to "...works out at tens of megaparsecs on this model; a different void model is worked at ARG-E09 and gives a tighter ~15 Mpc."

findings.problem: The TLDR opens "in the books it comes from it is a conclusion rather than a proof" and then names Rowbotham and Carpenter. That asserts a genealogy the entry deliberately declines to establish everywhere else: the module docstring says the Victorian works are offered because the argument "is in print thirty years before the Zion sermons", not as a route, and the refutation says of the Wallace/Collamore precedent "It is NOT offered as the route to the 461-item list"; the compression block likewise says of the Isaiah 45:18 clause-swap that "Whether that is a re-reading or an independent arrival is not established here, and the entry does not claim it." The TLDR claims it. Worse, this is now a visible self-contradiction on the skim path: I rendered docs/index.html and the C06 meta line reads "... items 69, 71, 73, 75, 419, 434 - first published by Wilbur Glenn Voliva" on the line immediately above "in the books it comes from". On a page whose product is provenance, the headline and the byline disagree in the same visual block.
findings.fix: Change the opening clause to a located-earliest claim rather than a descent claim: "This one is real, it is old, and in the earliest books located that carry it - Rowbotham 1865 and Carpenter 1885 - it is a conclusion rather than a proof." That is exactly what the entry proves and it removes the collision with the meta line.

findings.problem: The entry's central measurement is left open to the standard defence, and advocate.best_defense does not raise it. Section two derives the sine law and then produces Rowbotham's own Section 8 quotation of Phillips that the measured angle at the horizon "is identical" to the angle at the meridian. But Section 8's whole first half, which the entry quotes around rather than through, supplies the escape: Rowbotham argues that "when a light of any kind shines through a dense medium it will appear larger", and that near the horizon the Sun "must be dilated or enlarged" by the denser, damper air (Gutenberg #69892, lines 1832-1841). A defender concedes the geometric shrink and says atmospheric magnification cancels it - the observed constancy being the net. The entry's advocate block raises "you repurposed a footnote in a book you say is worthless" but never this, so the strongest reply to the entry's best evidence goes unanswered.
findings.fix: Add two sentences to section two closing the escape on real optics: near-horizon refraction does not magnify, it compresses - the Sun's vertical diameter is flattened by up to about 5 arcmin at the horizon while the horizontal diameter is unchanged, so the measured angle never grows and the required compensation runs the wrong way. Note also that the escape has to cancel a factor of twelve at 5 degrees, not a few per cent, and that the compensation would have to track altitude exactly on every clear day at every latitude. Then add the move to advocate.best_defense as a fifth hit so the rating is honestly earned.

findings.problem: "the 32-mile / 3,000-mile sun of the Zion catechism" attributes the figures to a document the cited chapter does not describe. In Schadewald's ch. 8 as served at cantab.net the string "catechism" occurs zero times, case-insensitive. The numbered question-and-answer material is Schadewald's own summarising device - "We will summarize some of them here to give the flavor of the whole" - applied to two named articles by Chester M. Shippey, "Answers to Common 'Proofs' that the Earth is a Globe" and "The True Shape of the Earth: A Practical Discussion". The 32-mile diameter is answer 3 and the 3,000-mile height is answer 4, both Shippey's. "Zion catechism" is our coinage for someone else's article, and it loses a named author on an entry about provenance. It appears in four published places: passage.gloss, refutation section two, verdict_challenge.reasoning, and the Schadewald source label.
findings.fix: Replace all four with the named attribution: "the 32-mile, 3,000-mile Sun of Chester M. Shippey's two Zion articles, as summarised by Schadewald in ch. 8". The refutation instance can read "Shippey's 32 miles across at 3,000 miles".

findings.problem: "Rowbotham says the same thing in the same order at the end of Section III, four hundred pages earlier in the argument." The page distance is impossible in the edition cited. The Internet Archive scan of the 1865 Simpkin, Marshall edition (identifier zeteticastronom00rowbgoog, imagecount 229) is a book of roughly 221 printed pages; in Gutenberg #69892 the Section III sentence ends at line 1582 and Section XIV opens at line 3692, an interval of about 44 per cent of the text, or roughly 95 pages. A four-hundred-page interval implies a book of 900-plus pages, and the nearest real object is the 1881 third edition at about 430 pages - which is exactly the edition confusion README.md and curmudgeon.md flag as recurring failure 3.
findings.fix: Delete the page figure and use the structural fact, which is the point anyway: "at the end of Section III, eleven sections earlier". If a page interval is wanted, "roughly a hundred pages earlier in a book of about 220".

findings.problem: "The page as served carries no byline" is false. summaries.summary: The argument presents six real CMB anomalies — hemispherical power asymmetry, the Cold Spot, point-parity, low variance, ISW correlations and a generic "isotropy violations" — as six independent witnesses to an Earth-centred cosmos, and Planck genuinely does call the existence of these features "uncontested", so the entry concedes them in full. It fails on agreement rather than on significance: two of the six are scalars with no direction at all, and the two that do carry directions sit 56° and 72° from the axis the argument is built on and 37° and 49° out of the ecliptic — computed from the coordinate labels printed on the figure the source itself reproduces at Galileo Was Wrong 7th ed., Vol. I p. 366, whose caption claims the axes form "an X and Y graph, with Earth at or very near the intersection point".

ARG-E04 welds two incompatible claims: Varshni's 1976 concentric quasar shells (spherical symmetry about Earth) and the Hutsemékers quasar-polarization alignment (a preferred axis) — joined in Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I p. 414 by the sentence "In other words, quasar distribution is centered around the Earth, just as Varshni had discovered." It fails twice over: Varshni's paper is a reductio arguing quasar redshifts are NOT cosmological (and 384 redshifts drawn at random produce 38–64 of the coincidence groups he counted 57 of, recomputed here), while the polarization signal is real, replicated and unexplained but rotates ~30°/Gpc and reverses handedness between galactic hemispheres — a set of directions, not a centre — and the "ecliptic" item traces to an ellipsis in Sungenis's quotation that deletes "the normal vectors to the planes determined by the quadrupole and the octopole", i.e. deletes the CMB from a sentence that was never about quasars.

The argument is that spiral galaxies show a left-handed excess in one sky hemisphere and a right-handed excess in the other, which Sungenis & Bennett (Galileo Was Wrong, 7th ed., Vol. I pp. 383-387) read as a "universal Coriolis force caused by the rotation and oscillation of the universe around the Earth." It fails twice: even at full strength the observable is a vector, and the caption to Fig. 1(a) of the very paper being cited (Longo, PLB 699:224) states that a universe with one global handedness looks right-handed on one side of ANY observer's sky and left-handed on the other — while the measurement itself falls to ~3.2σ once the axis is not assumed, has an opposite-sector asymmetry of 0.005 ± 0.032 in Longo's own data, sits 22° from the centre of the SDSS footprint against a stated 35° axis uncertainty, and has failed every independent re-analysis from Land et al. 2008 through Patel & Desmond 2024, who included Longo's own 15,158 galaxies and found "both Longo anomalies disappear" when monopole and dipole are fitted jointly.

The argument borrows the plane-of-satellites problem — a real, still-unresolved tension in galaxy formation published in Nature (Ibata 2013), Science (Müller 2018) and Nature Astronomy (Sawala 2023) — and reads it as evidence for a central Earth. It fails because every structure involved is referenced to other galaxies rather than to us: the Milky Way's satellite plane is inclined 65.5° to the ecliptic and Andromeda's 77.3° (recomputed in-session from published normals, self-checked against the 51° VPOS–GPoA inclination its authors publish), the two share no axis, Centaurus A's plane is centred on a galaxy 3.8 Mpc away, and the one genuinely Earth-facing feature — Andromeda's plane seen 3° from edge-on — is the condition for detecting its rotation at all, a selection effect quantified in 2026 by the plane proponents' own group.

The list asserts that the Pioneer and flyby anomalies point at the Earth and that this is cosmologically significant; the source it descends from — Sungenis & Bennett, Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II ch. 10 — says instead that "the resolution does not permit this assertion" and lists Earth-pointing as one of three (JPL's four) indistinguishable possibilities, mapping it to "a time signal anomaly" rather than to geocentrism. It fails because the Earth-direction was the mundane explanation's own advance prediction — the spin axis is aimed at Earth so the radio link closes, and ~63 W of one-sided radiation out of 2,578 W of RTG heat produces the whole Pioneer effect (Turyshev et al. 2012, "no anomalous acceleration remains") — while the flyby anomaly, which is genuinely still unexplained and is said so on the page, has as its only quantitative description a formula whose constant is 2ω⊕R⊕/c = 3.099×10⁻⁶, i.e. proportional to the Earth's sidereal rotation rate, and which mispredicted Juno 2013 (~6 mm/s expected, 0 ± 0.8 mm/s measured).

The argument takes the real, unresolved five-sigma disagreement between the SH0ES distance-ladder H0 (73.04 ± 1.04) and Planck+LCDM (67.4 ± 0.5) and reads the two live explanations for it — a distance-ladder systematic, or outflow from a local underdensity — as evidence that the Earth occupies a privileged position. It fails at a step nobody in the actual dispute contests: the "location" a void model can resolve is bounded by the CMB dipole to roughly 15 Mpc (about 49 million light-years, some 3.6e16 Earth diameters) around the Local Group, so the hypothesis cannot distinguish the Earth from Andromeda, its own leading advocate says "our galaxy" rather than "the Earth", and the two items are mutually exclusive escapes — if the tension is an observation bias there is no anomaly left to locate anyone with, and if it is a location bias the locating is done by a Lemaitre-Tolman-Bondi metric inside an expanding relativistic universe measured with the redshifts, standard candles and standard rulers other items on the same list reject.

Items 60 and 355 claim galaxy redshifts are quantized into spherical shells concentric on the Earth, compressing a real body of work — Tifft's ~72 km/s and Guthrie and Napier's ~37.5 km/s periodicities — through D. Russell Humphreys' 2002 shells derivation into Sungenis and Bennett's section "Galaxies: Spheres of Stars Centered Around the Earth". It fails on two independent grounds that do not require litigating the statistics: the periodicity is reported only in galactocentric or CMB-frame redshifts, so producing the signal means first subtracting the Earth's 29.79 km/s orbit and the Sun's 240 km/s galactic circuit (both numbers from Humphreys' own footnote 28), and the spatial-shell reading fails Humphreys' own smearing criterion by a factor of eight once peculiar velocities are put into his own redshift-to-distance equation.

Sungenis and Bennett argue that the Copernican principle is a philosophical assumption that pre-decides how every cosmological datum is read, so a central Earth is excluded by philosophy rather than evidence — and the premise is true, conceded in print by George Ellis and by the opening sentence of the very paper our record cites against it. It fails because the assumption was turned into a measurement: the source's own footnoted authority (Ellis, arXiv:1103.2335) lists four observational tests of the principle five pages before the sentence quoted from it, the kSZ power spectrum now bounds Gpc-scale radial inhomogeneity at about 1% per shell and overshoots the void models by two orders of magnitude, and even a total win would put us near the middle of a void tens of megaparsecs across in which the Earth still orbits the Sun.

The argument is that creation is ordered to man and the Sun is a servant lamp, therefore the Earth is central, flat or at rest — but in every source located it is a conclusion drawn after the geometry is supposedly established (Rowbotham 1865 reaches "secondary and subservient" through a "therefore" off a claimed triangulation; Carpenter prints "the heavenly bodies were made for man" after proof 100, not as one of them; Dubay's item 197 states it as a conditional answering a motive objection), while the list enters it as evidence. It fails on the merits because the one item with a physical consequence makes a checkable prediction — any small lamp at fixed height must shrink as the sine of its altitude — and Rowbotham's own Section 8 quotes an authority reporting that the Sun's measured angle at the horizon "is identical" to its angle at the meridian, while the anthropocentric premise, even granted whole, entails nothing about geometry (the tradition that held it hardest held the Earth to be a sphere, and on that physics the centre was the sump, not the throne).

The argument is that scripture describes an earth with sockets, a cornerstone and load-bearing pillars (Job 38:4-6, Job 9:6, Psalm 75:3, 1 Sam 2:8), so the ground rests on something and is not a free-floating globe; the source, Rob Skiba's 2015-2016 teaching document, states it at full strength in a section headed "Pillars of the Earth" and pre-emptively re-reads the standard counter-text, Job 26:7. It fails because the step from what an ancient poem pictures to what an instrument would find is supplied by the reader and by no verse, and because foundations do not discriminate disc from globe — the 1987 catalogue Skiba's own reading list points to files them under "Weaker Arguments" and reports the geocentrist movement's own astronomer citing the same verses to prove sphericity, while the movement's two named originators put incompatible things underneath (Rowbotham 1865: bottomless water; Skiba 2015: pillars).
